speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The information given by the Minister of Finance is-all I expected, and I am thankful to him,
I believe the House and the country will be interested in the figures he has given. The operation of the Mint has been, up to the present, somewhat mysterious and nobody seems to have known exactly what took place there. There are two points on which I have a word of comment. I understand the Minister of Finance expects that in a few years the Mint will be able to refine and dispose of all the gold produced in Canada either in the shape ol coin or bullion for export, but the hon. gentleman has no such expectation with regard to silver. The production of silver-in Canada is increasing from year to year until I think to-day Canada is the largest, producing silver country in the world. Up-to the present the American market is-the only market we have had for our silver, and it is sent to the United States in the shape of ore, not refined in this country. At present, all the silver produced in: Canada goes to New York, is refined in>
New York, and what is not consumed in. the United States is exported in bars to-European markets. Everyone who has travelled from New York to Liverpool knows that no inconsiderable part of the steamer's cargo is composed of silver bars shipped from New York to London, for distribution throughout Europe. Ten or twelve years ago, practically the whole of: that silver came chiefly from Colorado-and from other American territory, but at present a very large proportion of it comes from Cobalt. The Minister of Finance has-stated that the question of freight is the-impediment to the export of silver direct from Canada, and I would like to have some explanation from him on that point. I cannot see why the charges from Cobalt to Ottawa should be higher than from-Cobalt to New York, or the charges from: Ottawa to Liverpool higher than from New York to Liverpool.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Gold comes to the Mint by registered mail. So that from the Yukon it would come almost as cheaply as from points in the United States that are much nearer. If the silver production of Canada could all be exported to Great Britain, I think that my right hon. friend's point would be well taken. But, as the American market is an important market, he will see that there is more advantage in sending silver ore to New York to be refined and sold than in bringing it to Ottawa. I think that is what the deputy master of the Mint had in mind, and it was from him I got the information I am giving the committee. He pointed out also that private enterprise was engaged in the refining of silver, and he evidently had the view that was a consideration which should be borne in mind. Something, I have no doubt, has to be allowed for that. In addition to that, he pointed out, and I think with good reason, though it would not' be conclusive reason against the Government undertaking the operation, that the enterprise of silver refining on a large scale would require rather extensive operations involving a very costly plant entirely different in character from that which is utilized in the refining of gold which is of more limited quantity. These are the considerations which he laid before me and w7hich I lay before my right hon. friend and the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is a
technical subject, and one that requires a good deal of information. Of course, the American market is a large consuming market for gold. A good deal of the gold refined in New York is consumed in the United States and perhaps as large a proportion of it goes to Europe. But the silver to-day is shipped to the United States in the shape of ore. The freight ought to be much more considerable, I should say, than if the silver were refined in Canada and exported in bars. This seems true on the face of it because there is a lprge proportion of dross shipped with the silver in the ore, and freight has to be paid on all. It may be that we are not prepared to^ put up so costly a plant as the hon. minister refers to, and it may be that the market here is not sufficiently large to justify us in doing so. But I hope the day will come, and sooner rather than later, when we shall refine our own silver and consume it ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I
am glad to have the benefit of the views of my right hon. friend. This is a matter of much interest to the House and to the country and I shall be glad to pursue my investigations further in order to ascertain, if it be possible, whether the Government should undertake the refining of silver upon a large scale. This is a matter Sir WILFRID LAURIER,
of national importance, and I am entirely in sympathy with the view that, if possible, all refining of our own ores should be done in this country. This was drawn to my attention not long ago in connection with the question of export duty upon certain ores, and I found then that the question of a market was of supreme importance. The right hon. gentleman has rightly said that this is a technical question, but I desire to assure him that it has had and will continue to have my careful attention. I think that we are of one view and desire, that is, that this refining of our ores should be carried on in Canada. Our mineral production is increasing year by year in a most gratifying fashion, and I thiqk that that will be the history of the future as it has been of the past. It is obvious that having the minerals, our policy should be directed to the end of refining them here and doing everything we can to make them profitable.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance give expression to hi.s sentiments in favour of the refining in Canada of the precious metals produced in the four corners of our country, and also to hear him say that our Mint will eventually absorb all the gold we produce. This is a matter of very considerable importance. There is no doubt in my mind that our Pacific Coast cities lost a large amount of trade-in the early days of the Yukon because we had not the means in Canada of handling our gold. Everyone knows that there is practically no profit in handling gold of the standard fineness; it is the same as trading sovereigns. But we found in the Yukon that where the miners sell their gold they are very likely to buy their supplies-within a well-defined distance. If a man sold his gold in Ottawa he might or might not buy his supplies in Ottawa; but if he were a miner in the Yukon and sold his gold in Seattle he would be pretty sure to buy his supplies in Seattle. That is, considering Vancouver as against Seattle, where the miner sold his gold he would be likely to buy his supplies, unless the tariff on the goods were of a prohibitive character. I desire to ask the Minister of Finance how he expects the gold that we shall produce from time to time to be absorbed, over and above what we are now able to absorb, having in view the very large amount of American gold which is found in the vaults of our banks and government depositories.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

We hope it will be refined and sold in gold bars. I gave some figures when the matter was under consideration before, showing that we had sold fine gold bars during the calendar year 1912, to the amount of nearly $300,000. That could be increased in-

definitely. I pointed out, I think before my hon. friend came to the House this afternoon, that we were establishing a refinery at the Mint that would cost possibly $50,000 to improve and Increase the work in connection with our gold refining.

Do we
mint British sovereigns now?

I think not, as against
American gold, for while American gold is not of the same fineness as the British intrinsically it is of the same value. There may he times when British sovereigns are more in demand on the% occasion of a stringency or in some similar condition, but I do not see why they should be at a premium there generally.

They are at a premium
there now, and I understand that that is generally, if not always, the condition.

I am quite sure if we were to coin our own silver, it would be- accepted in the United States just as currently as the coins of that country.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. George H. Perley (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27, of the statutes of 1912, and to provide that whenever application is made to the Board of Grain Commissioners for the appointment of an inspecting officer or weighmaster, or both, at a place which is not a terminal point or a regular inspection point, the board, if satisfied that such an arrangement should be made and that the applicant is a responsible person, may order such arrangement as it deems proper, on condition that, besides the fees payable, the excess, if any, of the cost of carrying out such arrangement over the amount of such fees, shall be paid by the applicant in such manner and at such times as the board may determine; and that the provisions as to the inspection and weighing of grain, and as to the appointment of inspectors and weighmasters, and of any rules
and regulations made under the said provisions, shall apply at every place with respect to which such an arrangement has been made; and also that the annual license fee payable by the proprietor, lessee or manager of any terminal elevator shall be twenty-five dollars; the annual license fee payable by the owner of an elevator engaged in the manufacture of grain products in the western division, shall be five dollars; the annual license fee payable by the owner or lessee of a country elevator, shall be five dollars; the annual license fee payable by an applicant to carry on the business of gra_in commission merchant in the western division, shall be five dollars; and the annual license fee payable by any person to carry on the business of a track buyer, shall be five dollars.
(Mr. Bennett, East Simcoe, in the Chair.)

There are at present only two places in western Canada where there is a full equipment for the inspection of grain, namely, at the cities of Calgary and Winnipeg. When the Canada Grain Act was passed in this House a year ago, I urged upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce, now absent, the necessity for his taking to himself or to his Government power to duplicate that equipment for inspection at any other place which the Governor in Council, the Minister or the Grain Commission should deem it advisable to do so. The minister said it would be a comparatively easy matter to have the Act changed from session to session or from time to time. In the city of Moosejaw it has been felt for some months -indeed, I might almost say for a year or two-that that city ought to be made a general inspection point. The policy of the present Government and the operation of the Grain Commission may result in the establishment in certain centres in the West of internal storage elevators, and in those elevators there will be stored grain which will be made the subject of security by the farmers, because it will have received its final inspection and gTade certificate will have been granted. But a final certificate as to the grade of the grain cannot be obtained unless there is available a full equipment for the purposes of inspection, and, as the minister is now amending the Act-, and especially as he is touching this very feature to which I refer, I think this would be the proper time for the Government to take to itself the power to create at any other point, as may be deemed desirable, a full equipment for the inspection of grain. I have reference especially to the Survey Board, which is the board of appeal, and is really the authority when any dispute arises as to the grade of the grain. I do not at this moment urge that the Government should establish a full equipment at Moosejaw or Regina or

any other particular point, strong as my views may ibe in that direction, but, as I have said, I think the Government should, under the Grain Act, take to itself power to create, if the occasion should arise, a full inspection equipment at Moosejaw or any other city, and that they should not have their hands tied in that regard. The Grain Commission nnder Professor McGill has carried on negotiations with the Board of Trade of the city of Moosejaw, as a result of which there may be a proposition, mutually agreeable to the Grain Commission and to the citizens of Moosejaw. by which an internal storage elevator shall be constructed in that city. In this case the trouble will be that the Grain Commission or the Government will say to the city of Moosejaw: We have no power to establish in your city a full equipment for inspection, because the Act specifies that this shall be done only at Calgary and Edmonton. I therefore strongly, yet respectfully urge upon the minister that he should endeavour to take such steps as I have advised; otherwise the hopes which are being raised in Moosejaw in this regard wifi never be fulfilled, because we cannot have an equipment of this kind unless the hands of the Government are free to act. The procedure involved in coming to Parliament for this authority is cumbersome and fraught with delay, and I think that in connection with this proposed amendment of the Grain Act there should be some provision whereby the establishment in other cities aside from those which are already grain inspection points-of the inspection equipment that we are so desirous of obtaining at Moosejaw will be made possible.
Mr. PERLEY; I think that so far as internal elevators are concerned, my hon. friend is unnecessarily alarmed. The matter of building internal terminal elevators is being considered by the Government at this time, and I hope to be able to make an announcement in that regard in the near future. Any internal terminal elevators built on the prairies will he constructed, as I understand the matter, under section 13 of the Canada Grain Act, which gives the Governor in Council power to authorize the minister to construct, acquire, lease or expropriate any terminal elevator after Parliament has granted the money for such purpose. The terminal elevator when built would come under the Interpretation Act, which covers any point declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal. In other words, if it were decided to build an interior terminal elevator at Moosejaw, Regina or Saskatoon, this point would be declared by Order in Council to be a terminal; then it would be subject to the clauses in the Act which provide for the inspection of grain in and out of terminals, so I think that covers Mr. KNOWLES.
the point in connection with interior terminal elevators.
No.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I quite, understand that
it would not provide inspection points without terminal elevators, but if a terminal elevator were built at any one of these places, provision is made in the Act for the inspection of the grain in and out of the terminal elevator at whatever point may be declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal elevator.
Mr. KNOWLES; Does the minister mean that it would be feasible to have grain stored in a terminal and certificates granted four hundred miles away from where there is a terminal ? Would that be feasible ?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I would be glad to talk this over with my hon. friend privately, but, as I understand, there is a provision in the Act in the clause with regard to terminal elevators under which all the machinery would be provided for weighing the grain in and out of interior terminal elevators. If Parliament granted the money for that purpose and if it were decided by Order in Council that any point was to have a terminal elevator, then the machinery would be provided under the Act for inspection and weighing of grain in and out of that elevator. If that is not so I am mistaken and I certainly think it should be corrected.

I would not be positive, but I think that it is distinctly limited to two cities which are both about the same distance from Moosejaw, four hundred miles, and, of course, further from other places. I submit it would be an anomaly, an absurdity almost, to have a terminal elevator at a place four hundred or five hundred miles away from where you have a survey board.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that if, by Order in Council, a city were declared a terminal, money provided by Parliament, and an interior elevator built at that point, that there is no machinery under the Act by which provision could be made for weighing grain in and out of that elevator by persons on the spot P
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to look it up and let me have the reference in order that I may inquire into it before the Bill comes up for second reading. This is merely a resolution which would not affect the matter which the hon. gentleman is discussing.

I mean that there is no full equipment. There is provision by which men can be employed at any place directed by Order in Council who would

do inspecting, but the inspection to be of any use must be final and permanent and the inspection that such a man would do would be so obvious that the farmers themselves could do it. It is on the nice points that the inspection really makes a difference and it is only where there is a survey board that it is possible to have these fine distinctions decided.

I wish to emphasize what my hon. friend has said. The Canada Grain Act, as I understand it, simply makes provision for terminal facilities at Calgary and at Winnipeg, and the point I wish to take, which has been already taken by the hon. member for Moosejaw, is that if the Government intend to establish interior storage elevators or terminal elevators at other points in the centre of the prairie provinces, some provision should be made for it in the Act. The Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to section 13 of the Canada Grain Act. I do not know what would be the proper construction to place on the section, but I know the intention in my mind when it was discussed before Parliament last year was that that section simply applied to terminal facilities at Calgary and at Fort William. That was the understanding I had and I think that is a proper construction to place on section 13 of the Act. Therefore, if we are to have terminal facilities at other places besides Calgary, Winnipeg and Fort William, some provision must be made for it in the Canada Grain Act, and the general impression is that there is no power in the Government to establish these terminal facilities properly as at Calgary, Winnipeg and Fort William. Notwithstanding that fact there have been a number of meetings held by the present Grain Commission in different parts of western Canada, I remember a meeting at Regina and I saw reports of meetings at Moosejaw, Saskatoon and Humboldt. I do not know whether the commission was properly reported or not Wht I know the impression was left in the minds of the people there that interior storage elevators would be established at every one of these places throughout Saskatchewan where the Grain Commission held meetings. Some of these people are going to be disappointed. The hon. member for Moosejaw has continually advocated on the floor of this House the necessity of some terminal facility at Moosejaw. Equal necessity exists at Regina and other places in Saskatchewan if we are to get the full benefit of the Grain Act.
I wish again to refer to the question of the necessity for increasing the fees as provided for in the resolution. I am not sure whether on the former occasion the minister gave us certain figures to substantiate the
necessity of raising these fees or not, but I have been informed on reliable authority that the administration of the Canada Grain Act, as far as the western division of Canada was concerned, did produce quite a considerable surplus during the last fiscal year. The amount given to me was some $57,000 but it was stated that the eastern division was run at such a loss as to necessitate the minister bringing down the present resolution increasing the fees for terminal licenses and elevator licenses in general throughout the western division of Canada. It is possible that I may have been misinformed but I call the attention of the minister to this fact that it is not out of the elevator companies that these fees will come; they must of necessity come out of the grain trade and therefore of necessity out of the pockets of the producers of grain because it is a well known fact that all fees charged and all freight rates must- of necessity come out of and be added to the cost of the production of grain on the prairie of the West. If 1 have been misinformed in regard to these figures I would like to have the correct information from the minister, because if my information is not correct there is a misunderstanding in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that I have not the figures as between the East and the West. I suppose that they could be obtained but the Canada Grain Act is being administered by the Grain Commission as a whole. The information given me regarding this increase of fees is as follows:
The fee of $2 does not yield enough to pay for the cost of printing the licences and forms, mailing them and the rules and regulations, and recording them in the office. The elevators have hitherto been administered through the warehouse commissioners office and the license fees were the only source of revenue. The result was that the office showed a large deficit every year. If the grain department is to pay its way the license fees must be increased.
So far as the increase of the fee from $2 to $5 would affect the price paid by the elevator or the track buyer, it seems to me that it need hardly be considered.
I doubt very much whether it would affect the price a fraction of a cent.

The hon. minister
asked me if I could refer him to the section referring to the Grain Survey Board. The sections are Nos. 101 and 102. Section 101 provides for the way in which the grain is inspected.
Do these sections not deal more with appeals?
Yes.
As they stand now would they not be sufficient for the purpose of establishing a terminal elevator at Maose-jaw or at. any other point?

It is true that the sections referred to do apply to cases under appeal, but to the other questions of my hon. friend I would say no. It is not feasible to have twelve gentlemen, _ some of whom live in Calgary and some in Winnipeg, 400, 500 or 600 miles away from the seat of the terminal elevator, dealing with the matter in contention.

I understand my hon.
friend to say that it would foe impossible to have a new terminal at Moosejaw or at the other place unless the Act was changed. It may be inconvenient and impracticable, but it is not impossible.

I did not say it was impossible. The Act provides that a terminal elevator could be established at Moosejaw or at Prince Albert, but it is an absurdity to think of establishing one at either of these places when the Survey Board is so far away. I will read section 101:
Whenever, in a division or district from which a grain survey hoard has been appointed, the owner or possessor of any grain inspected therein is not satisfied with the inspecting officer's grading of such grain, he may appeal therefrom to the chief inspector, who shall view a proper sample of the grain respecting which the grading is in dispute, drawn or secured in a manner satisfactory to him, and give his decision thereon, which shall be final unless the owner or possessor, within twenty-four hours after receiving the notification thereof, makes further appeal to the grain survey board for the division or district, in which case the said board shall give a final decision to settle the grading of the grain in dispute; but nothing in this section shall prevent the owner or possessor of the said grain appealing directly from the inspecting officer to the said board, whose decision in all cases shall be final and binding on all parties, and the inspecting officer shall issue a certificate accordingly. If the owner or possessor so desires he may call for a fresh sample to be drawn by the inspector for use on re-inspection or survey, the expense thereof to be borne by the applicant, and in case it be drawn for the purpose of survey it shall be sent to the secretary of the said board.
The next sub-section is in regard to cases in which there shall be no further appeal, and the third sub-section deals with the cost of appeal. Then section 102 reads:
The grain survey board for the division shall consist of twelve persons, of whom six shall be nominated by the Board of Trade of the city of Winnipeg, two by the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Manitoba, two by the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Alberta, and two by the Commissioner of Agriculture for the province of Mr. KNOWLES.
Saskatchewan. The competency of the persons so nominated must be approved by the board.
The next sub-section of this clause provides that the board may make further regulations, and the third sub-section has reference to the taking of the oath. Section 103 deals with the by-laws, and section 104 is the same as 102, providing for an office in Winnipeg and another in Calgary. It would be a simple thing for the minister to make a provision not that the survey board should be either at Calgary or Winnipeg or Moosejaw, because we must prove the merits of our claim to have a board at each of these cities, but to see that the Government's hands will not be tied. I do not think it is out of the way to ask that.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I think I understand now what my hon. friend means. He is referring entirely to the survey board, which is the court of appeal in respect to the inspection and weighing of grain. If the Government by Order in Council decided to make Moosejaw or Saskatoon, or Regina a terminal point, the clauses in this Act from 122 on, relating to terminal elevators, make provision for the manner of inspecting grain at such elevators. If there was an appeal from the inspection, that appeal would have to go to Winnipeg. This question has never been raised before, but I ask my hon. friend, would it be possible to have an effective system of appeals with a lot of different appeal boards? How are we going to get consistency in inspection unless we confine ourselves to one or two appeal boards? If there were a terminal elevator in the city represented by my hon. friend, and there were provision there for weighing and inspecting the grain-as a rule I suppose that the inspection is satisfactory and that there are not many appeals-if there were appeals from the inspection at that terminal elevator, would it not be better to have them go to the board to which went the appeals from other elevators? Would it not be better to have the boards of survey limited to two, for instance. Would the system not be much more perfect to havb the grain from all parts of the West graded in the same way?

No, I think not. It
would be just as easy to get a competent board in the wheat cities, as in Winnipeg or Calgary, perhaps easier.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Is it a fact that there are not many appeals?

I think the percentage of appeals is small, speaking off hand, but I repeat that the cases that are of moment and that require authentic inspection are the cases that are appealed. That is the point I wish to make. I think that the fact that we have two boards already disposes of the precious doctrine of uniformity. If we have two boards we might as well have

three. At Moosejaw we might have a -better board than the one at Calgary, because Moosejaw is in the wheat country, and the board there would be less apt to make mistakes than the boards in Calgary or Winnipeg. At Moosejaw we have a population more familiar with the grain situation than the population of the two other cities.
There is another point to which I wish to call the attention of the minister. I would refer him to section 57, sub-section 2 of the Act, which reads as follows:
Notwithstanding any other provision in this Act that may conflict therewith, sample markets may be established in the cities of Winnipeg, Tort William and Calgary, and the mixing of grain permitted in connection therewith, under such rules and regulations as are recommended by the board and approved by the Governor in Council.
I wish to press upon the minister and the Government the necessity of having the same provision placed in the Act here as I advocated in connection with the survey board. Parliament thought it wise that sample markets should be established at Calgary, Winnipeg and Fort William. If that appeared to be wise, then I say it would be just as wise to establish one in any other city than Winnipeg, Calgary or Fort William. I come from Moosejaw, a city in which there is far more justification for establishing a sample market than in the city of Calgary, and I will tell the minister wh}^. If a sample market has any effect it is because there are buyers to patronise it. Any hon. gentleman who comes from the prairie provinces will agree that the buyers in the sample market will be the Americans from Minnesota.
Why was it placed at Calgary and Winnipeg?	,
Because the Government submitted that in the Bill, we passed it, and there was no way by which we could prevent it.
I understand it was because grain going west would go through Calgary and grain going east would go through Winnipeg.

I think that was the reason, but I submit that that reason had not been thought out to its logical conclusion. I think that everybody who comes from the West will agree that the Minnesota buyers are the people who are fondest of the sample market, and who like to buy on that market. They are accustomed to it, they have formed that business habit in their own country and if ever a sample market is a success it will be because it is patronised by the Americans. I submit that Moosejaw is the place where a sample market would supply the Minnesota people very much better than would the city of Calgary. It is a city having direct railway
connection with St. Paul and Minneapolis. We have four passengers trains daily between Moosejaw, St. Paul and Minneapolis, and there are freight trains in great numbers every day. It is a direct line, and it is at a city like Moosejaw that a sample market should be established. There is no reason why the Government should not take power to itself to establish sample markets at any place that circumstances might justify their establishment. There is more justification for a sample market at Moosejaw than at any other place on the prairie because of the railway facilities between that place and the two great milling cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis. I would press upon the minister that, when he is amending this Act, he keep in mind the desire of the city of Moosejaw for a sample market.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I shall be glad to take
the matter into consideration.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. acting Minister of Trade and Commerce to an abuse that has arisen in connection with hospital elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. I am told that the intention of the hospital elevator was to take care of and cure damaged wheat. I understand that there are eight or nine -elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur licensed as hospital elevators with the result that they may take in any kind of grain, damaged or otherwise, and mix it to their heart's content. Then, under section 124 of the Act, they are entitled, in fact, the grain board is compelled to give them, a certificate for whatever grade the inspector thinks right. In the ordinary elevator there is a strict account kept of all the grades of wheat that go in and at the end of the season you are able to check out and compare the grades they have sold as compared with the grades they have received, and see whether they have kept an accurate and honest account. The effect of licensing these elevators as hospital elevators is practically to vitiate all the sections of the Act. The hospital elevator may have ninety per cent of damaged grain, it may mix it with straight grade grain and then it is entitled to demand of the inspector a certificate of the product -of -the elevator whatever it is. I have had the complaint made to me that dozens and dozens of cars have come down to eastern Ontario certified as straight grade wheat by the inspector, although this grain was the product of the hospital elevators. Great damage .has been done the eastern millers by reason of the operations of the hospital elevators. They say that if there are to he hospital elevators they should keep some account of the wheat that comes into their possession and compare that with the wheat that is turned

out. Then, further, they say that they should be allowed to sell by sample and that the inspector should not be compelled to give a straight grade certificate. I would like to call the minister's attention to this matter because it seems to be a very serious defect in the Act. It appears to permit that to be done which it was the intention of the Act to prevent.
These hospital elevators are, under the Act, terminal elevators, I understand?

Under the provision of the Act, as I read it, every hospital elevator is a terminal elevator. That is the peculiar feature of the Act, because the Act says:
' Hospital elevator ' includes every elevator or warehouse which is used for the cleaning or other special treatment, of rejected or damaged grain and which is equipped with special machinery for that purpose.
Any terminal elevator which treats a little damaged grain is a hospital elevator. If the word 'only' were inserted after the word 'grain' it could be restricted. But under the Act it would appear that any terminal elevator is a hospital elevator, and vice versa.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Section 124
reads as follows:
There may be such number of hospital elevators as are determined by the board, which shall be governed by such regulations and restrictions as are imposed by the board.
I would imagine that the board could make regulations to prevent the very thing of which my hon. friend complains. If there has been any mixing of grain to the detriment of the public, I am surprised that no report of it was made to the minister. It seems that the case is covered by the Act and that the matter can be regulated.

There have been no regulations made. If my right hon. friend looks at subsection 3 he will see that it reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, .	.
grain which is being shipped out from a hospital elevator shall, at the request of the owner or possessor thereof, or of his authorized agent, be inspected and graded and the grade so arrived at shall be the grade thereof.
It nullifies all the other provisions of the Act,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It can be inspected and graded, but I would suppose that the inspection would be regulated by the board itself.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I would suggest to my
hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro), that, if he would be good enough to write a letter to the department, I will Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
see that it is sent to the Board of Grain Commissioners with a request to have the matter investigated.

When the Bill was under consideration the possibility of what my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) complains of occurring was brought to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It was urged upon his attention that the Act should make provision to prevent just what has occurred. The grain that goes into the hospital elevators for treatment is, under this section, graded as it comes out without regard to its having been treated. The contention from this side of the House was that grain, which had gone into an hospital elevator for treatment, should be earmarked as having been treated. The present provision in the law has proven to be injurious to the trade and it vitiates to a great degree the attempt of the Act to prevent mixing of grain. I would urge the minister to take the matter up with the grain commission, and if the facts are established, as I believe they are, opportunity should be taken this session to make the necessary provisions that grain which has gone through an hospital elevator shall have the fact of its being treated grain stated on the certificate.

Either that or it
should not be given a government certificate.
Whatever the commission may decide is the proper thing to do may be done.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Last summer there was a great deal of damaged grain which could not be treated at the ordinary hospital elevator, and to help the owners of that grain the Government allowed an American floating drying elevator to go to Port Arthur for a certain length of time to treat that Canadian grain. The grain did not belong to the floating elevator; so much a bushel was paid for treating it by the owners. When that grain was treated by the elevator and came out, if the inspectors knew their business and put it in the proper grade, is it fair to the owners of the grain to have that grain earmarked as having been treated? If it is earmarked as treated grain, it seems to me the farmers in the northwest would suffer eventually. Does my hon. friend think that his idea would work out in that case?

The hon. gentleman is
putting up the case of the dealer who owned the grain when it was treated against that of the miller or consumer who buys the grain after being treated. We want to do everything we can to give the holder of western grain the best price he can reasonably get for it so that the farmer from whom he buys may also get the best price. But the

whole purpose of the Grain Act is to prevent grain passing to the ultimate consumer under false pretences as to its quality, believing that in the end the initial producer will suffer because of that. The contention is that this treated grain is graded without certificate as being treated grain, but that is only part of the story. The essential part is that the whole purpose of the Act as contained in these other sections, which are directed against the possibility of mixing different grades of grain, are rendered ineffective so far as these hospital elevators aTe concerned, because under this unrestricted section mixing can be carried on in connection with these hospital elevators to an unlimited degree. The possibility of mixing is introduced in contravention of the whole spirit of the Act.

I point out the inconsistency between section 124 and a portion of section 107, which portion reads:
No. 3 wheat and lower grades rejected for smut and scoured shall be graded as scoured of the grade to which it belongs:	Provided
that wheat which is inspected No. 3 northern scoured, or lower, may be graded in such regular grade, not higher than No. 3, as the inspector determines.
That shows that No. 3 going into any other elevator can never come out more than No. 3; but No. 3 going into an hospital elevator can come out as No. 1 Northern hard, and the inspector is bound to give a certificate irrespective of the fact that it went into the hospital elevator.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Suppose wheat that had not been damaged would have graded as No. 1 Northern but it gets damaged and has to be dried; I would like to know whether or not the methods of inspection applied to this wheat which has been so dried are sufficient to reveal the precise and actual damage it suffered by having got wet, so that that damage can be taken into account in giving the inspection certificate.

The inspection having
been made only as to the exterior of the grain, it does not reveal the fact that the grain has suffered internal damage by reason of having got wet and having been dried. That militates against its ultimate milling value. The grain has suffered a permanent damage by reason of its condition which it does not altogether recover from intrinsically, although it does in appearance; I think that is an established fact. But it is not because of the ineffectiveness of the inspection of the treated grain as giving information to the miller, that the great objection is. It is because it is as though every door were closed against mixing except in the hospital elevator, and there the doors were
thrown wjde open; and the result is that it is not only the treated grain that is affected under the inspection, but all the efforts of the Act to prevent mixing are affected so far as grain that can be put through these hospital elevators is concerned.
Mr. W. -M. MARTIN (Regina):	I am
glad to hear a complaint coming from an Ontario man, the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) with respect to the marketing of western grain. It has appeared to me sometimes to be the idea of a number of members in this House that the representatives from the West ventilate their grievances too often. Apparently, there are grievances regarding the marketing of western grain which affect the people in Ontario. I would suggest to the hon. member for North Grey that he urge upon i?e	Minister and the Government
the advisability of carrying out one of the promises made to the people before the last election, that is, the promise of the Government ownership of terminal elevators. I can well remember a resolution moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) who at that particular stage in his political career was very active in urging the interests of the farmers of western Canada. It was to the effect that the Government should acquire, by expropriation or otherwise, these elevators. That resolution was voted for by every member in the House who is now in the House supporting the Government. I could quote to the House the number of statements that the right hon. Prime Minister made when he took his western tour in July, I think it was, 1911. I remember hearing him at the meeting in Regina, and a very good meeting it was too. He used the expression that if his party were returned to power, and forced to undertake the responsibilities of the Government of this country, they would proceed to take over the terminal elevators. There are also men in western Canada, like the hon. member for Souris, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) and others who surelv are not satisfied with the Government's fulfilment of that pledge. For we find that all the Government has done up to the present time is to prepare to make one terminal elevator, I thought at Fort William, but I see in ' Hansard ' that it is given as Port Arthur-in any case, at the head of the lakes. And they are proposing an appropriation for a contract to build .an elevator on a piece of land of thirty-seven acres which they have acquired. I saw also the report in the Regina Province of a speech of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) at a banquet last June, in which he said that before the crop moved for 1912, the terminal ele-

vator was going to be completed. I am not repeating what I saw in Liberal newspapers, but I can show that statement reported in the Regina Province, a Conservative newspaper and one that is very active on behalf of this Administration^ I do not wish to open this whole question about terminal elevators, but there must be members from western Canada who are not satisfied with the fulfilment of the Government pledge on that subject. I find in the manifesto issued by the Prime Minister before the last election, this:
The control and operation by the state of the terminal elevators.
But the policy of the Government is apparently to control and operate one elevator at Fort William or Port Arthur. I would refer to the statement made by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) in answer to a question to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Mc-Craney):
Has the Government under contemplation the establishment of a terminal elevator system under Government control?
Mr. Perley:	We are building a large elevator at Port Arthur at the present time for the purpose of controlling the rates, to a certain extent at all events, and so on. The further construction of elevators at Fort William has not been considered up to the present time.
So, apparently, it was considered before this Government came into power in 1911, but according to the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, it has not been considered since during all this time. So, I suppose, that all they intend to do to fulfil the pledge they gave in 1911 in regard to the ownership of terminal elevators is to build and operate one elevator at Fort William.

ment of grain at the terminal elevator points. I would like to ask the hon. minister if any modification has been made in the policy of the Government with regard to the moisture tests on corn. speechtext:
A deputation made up

The view I take of this resolution depends a great deal on what I think of the board. The legislation we propose in this resolution says that the board may determine so and so, and I, as the representative of 135,000 people of the West, feel it my duty to find out something about those to whom we are giving authority so to determine. I find myself very much in the dark when the Government declines to tell us who compose the board, and whether the board has its full complement or not. I do not raise the point for the purpose of debating ycrnr ruling, Mr. Chairman; whether I think your ruling is right or wrong, I am sure it is given after a long parliamentary experience, and that it is honest and sincere. But I feel very much handicapped in the matter because, although there is much in this resolution with which I cannot quarrel and which I might desire to support, I am opposed to the resolution so long as the appointments are under the control of a board over which there hangs so serious a cloud of suspicion. *Further, we must vote without even the information as to who composed the board, and when the minister is asked whether a man of the common name of Jones is a member of the board and refuses to give the answer it is another form of gag. The minister cannot deny that it is a reasonable request to ask whether Mr. Jones is on the board or not. But he says he will not give that information and for the moment he has the power and we will have to bow to it.
Mr. ROBB.
I want to read what the right hon. the Prime Minister said at Portage la Prairie in 1911. I shall read it very deliberately in order that the Prime Minister may hear it clearly. He said:
I have arrived at

Not I am coming, mind you, but I have arrived.
-at the conclusion

-that the result can only be attained by
state control and operation of terminal elevators.
By ' state ' I presume he means, not provincial authorities, not the Imperial authorities, not the Right Hon. Mr. Winston Churchill; he undoubtedly means the body created by the British North America Act, this Parliament.
-by state control and operation of the terminal elevators.
You will mark the plural. If it came to a quibble, and I do not accuse the Prime Minister of quibbling, but it is ' elevators,' not ' elevator.' He is not going to reach a solution of this difficulty by purchasing 37-2 acres of land near Fort William, it is by acquiring elevators, not by buying land.
We trust to carry out that policy without delay if returned to power.
Let me dwell on these two words ' without delay.' You know there has been a good deal of contention about the exact meaning of the speedy construction of a navy, the dispute arising on the interpretation of ' speedy.' We here have the words ' without delay.' The Prime Minister delivered that speech many times in the Northwest and travelling around through our beautiful prairie provinces he had plenty of time to think just what he would say, and he used the words ' without delay ' time after time and after mature consideration as to what words he should use.
Let me now read the whole extract in order that it may sink in:
I have arrived at the conclusion that the result can only be attained by state control and operation of the terminal elevators. We trust to carry out that policy without delay if returned to power.
Twenty months have gone by, and ' without delay ' stares the Prime Minister in the face. At Battleford the Prime Minister clinched the whole thing by these words:
If it should be the will of the people of Canada to impose upon me the great respon-

sibility of being called upon to form a government in Canada, and after that government has been formed, the policy I have outlined will be carried out by the Government as I have stated, or one_ man of the Government will go out of public life.
The right hon. gentleman on that occasion told the people that he was born a British subject, had lived a British subject and would die a British subject, and many-other things which did not concern them very much ; we will be able to find all that information in an encyclopedia forty years hence. But they did take a most abiding and vital interest in the promise to construct elevators without delay and they -naturally had a right to take him at his word when he said: When I get into power the policy I have pointed out will be carried out or one man will go out of public life in Canada. Let us realize once for all that the Prime Minister of this country occupies a responsible position and that promises made by him cannot be lightly broken. The people of the West have one hundred and fifty million or two hundred million dollars worth of grain to put through the -elevators every year. The Prime Minister pledged himself that it was not only his firm intention to carry out his promise, but if that promise was not fulfilled he would go out of public life :and here after more than twenty mouths, twenty-two months, it will be two years in two months, the Prime Minister has done absolutely nothing. I say it with all respect, in the way of obtaining control and operation of terminal elevators. If we are going to renew and extend the powers of this board under the Grain Act, when we have this feature of our legislation before us, our grain legislation, it is fair to ask the Prime Minister what he intends to do about these promises now, promises that he has not carried out ' without delay.' I wish for the sake of my constituents, he would enlighten us on the subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no doubt that the twenty months to which my hon. friend has alluded, or the twenty-two months-for his arithmetic is not much better than his logic-have seemed very long to my hon. friend, therefore I do not at all complain of his bringing to the attention of the House the observations to which he has alluded, and which he seems to have treasured up in a bound volume. I hope he will commit its contents to his memory because The quotations which he jnade from it were very much the better part -of his speech. I would point out that, in the very first session in which this Government met Parliament, we made provision for building a three and a quarter million bushel state-owned ' elevator at Port Arthur, that the contract was let for that
a good many months ago, the building is now under construction and, as I understand the elevator is expected to be ready to receive this season's crop. Under those circumstances I could hardly expect my hon. friend to admit that there has been a fair beginning but I know that if he would look over some of the records of the past, to which I shall not do more than allude, he would be convinced not only that it is a fair beginning but that it is a very good, a very excellent beginning. My hon. friend before the close of the session will find that we will be prepared to make some advance upon that policy this year. State-owned elevators were very much in demand in the western part of this country for the reason that the people thought that they were not getting fair play in the inspection and the certificating of their grain. It was urged that certain evils and abuses that were spoken of very often in this House could be brought to a conclusion by a system of state-owned elevators better and more effectually than in any other way.
I was impressed and many hon. gentlemen in this House were impressed with that view. Perhaps the subsequent record with regard to the efficiency of grain inspection may, to a certain extent, have modified the views of some hon. gentlemen in this House with regard to the absolute necessity of state-ownership- but whether that be so or not we did proceed at the very first session when we met Parliament to make a respectable beginning of that policy which is being carried out to-day. When my hon. friend speaks of delay I would ask him to contrast the progress which we have made in respect of the pledge to which I have alluded with the progress which was made in some fifteen years of' the period when his party were in power.
That is easy.

My right hon. friend
wishes to contrast the progress which was made in fifteen years by the late Government with the progress that his Government has made in less than two years. The difference is that there was no promise made before the fifteen years, and there was a promise made before the two years. I ask him how long he expects his Government to remain in power?
Mr. BORDEN. About twenty-five years.

My right hon. friend just about gives the time. It will take twenty-five years at the present rate to fulfill that promise. I do not think that will be considered satisfactory by the people who are



interested in the Government operation of elevators. I am sorry to see my right hon. friend and his followers treating this matter with such levity. The question of the handling of the great source of annual wealth of this country, and of the economical handling of it so that that product will reach the markets of the world in the best condition, is in itself important, hut surely the promise of the leader of the Government of Canada is even more important and is^ something that should not be treated with levity. The promise not only has not been made good, but there has been no indication during the eighteen months that have elapsed since the Government came into power of any intention to make it good.
_ You have ruled, Sir, that this question of the personnel of the grain commission is not a fair subject of discussion at this particular stage, but I would like to say that in my humble judgment the presentation of the resolution which provides for the fixing of fees and for the placing of a special and hitherto non-existent authority in the hands of the commissioners is the time when the merit of those commissioners should properly be discussed. My hon. friend the minister made one Temark which requires a little analysis. If the hon. minister did not think that I meant that his Government could do nothing right-of course they do some things right, and my hon. friend is all right, but he has not charge of the department and is lost, and some of the other departments are not all right-I do not think he meant what he said about the late Government. speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend will acknowledge that we improved it.

You may have put in a comma or a semi-colon, but I do not -know of any point which you improved. My hon. friends opposite tried tiheir level best to ruin it. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister seems to be less an advocate of Government control and operation of terminal elevators now than he was in 1911. He says that certain things have come to light which have modified his views. The Prime Minister, when he made that tour through the prairies, said to the people, in gravity and seriousness, that if he was returned to power he would give them without delay government operation and control of terminal elevators. Let him say what he likes, he has not answered that point. To-day he seems to be less along the pathwa5>- leading to government control and operation of terminal elevators than ever because he says that certain things have occurred which have modified his views. We expected that when he started on that pathway he would go right along, but he has gone backwards. He is like the man that Goldsmith tells us about who, going along the road, becoming tired and wanting to rest himself, jumped upon the back of a cart going the other way. In the official Hansard of the British House ' of Commons, which I have now before me. Here is the report I read in the evening:
Both these views seem to me to be equally wrong and equally harmful to our interests, and I must repeat that the Canadian ships are absolutely necessary for the whole world defence of the British Empire from the end of 1915 or from the beginning of 1916, onwards.

Mr. Clark:	The words which my hon.

I have here the official parliamentary debates of the House of Commons of Great Britain of March 31, 1913; in other words, the English Hansard, and I desire, in confirmation of the report which I read to the House from the Montreal Star, and as to its very wording, a confirmation of the cable, a part of which 1 read to the House on the evening of April 8, last, and as to which my hon. friend from Red Deer stated he would require further confirmation, because it was in contradiction, he said, of everything that had been said by the right Hon. Winston Churchill and the cabinet for many years past. I desire to read from the English Hansard the statement made by the Right Hon. It is necessary, however, to make it clear that these three ships under discussion in Canada are absolutely required from 1916 onwards for the whole world defence of the British Empire, apart altogether from the needs of Great Britain in home waters; that they will play a real part in the defence of the Empire, and that, if they fail, a gap will be opened to fill which further sacrifices will have to be made without undue delay by others.
My hon. friend says that what I originally quoted was a garbled thing; I will quote what he described as a garbled thing. It is this:
The three ships were absolutely required for the whole world defence of the British Empire apart from England. They would play a real part in Imperial defence and if they are not forthcoming steps will have to be taken to fill the gap and the strain of the burden would have to be placed upon others.
I will read again the words of Winston Churchill from the British ' Hansard,' and you can contrast them with the citation I gave from Mr. Churchill on April 18:
It is necessary however, to make it clear that the three ships now under discussion in Canada are absolutely required from 1916 onwards for the whole world defence of the British Empire, apart altogether from the needs of Great Britain in home -waters; that they will play a real part in the defence of the Empire; and that, if they fail, a gap will be opened to fill which further sacrifices will have to be made without undue delay by others.
The Right Hon. Mr. Churchill goes on to say:	i
i
With these facts in view. I ask the House-seriously : Is it not unwise for some people-on one side of the House to say that the Canadian ships are redundant, superfluous a"! an unnecessary burden-(Hon. Members:	Noland is it not equally unwise for other people on the other side to say that they ought to be i-edundanr superfluous, and an unnecessary burden. Both these views seem to me to be equally wrong and equally harmful to our interests, and I must repeat that the Canadian ships are absolutely necessary for the -whole world defence of the British Empire from the end of 1915, or from the beginning of 1916 onwards.
These are the precise words that I quoted from my cable. Mr. Churchill continues :
The fact that they are necessary is no measure of their value. Their value far exceeds the value of three ships. We can build three-ships ourselves if necessary. Parliament has never refused to supply the money for that which responsible ministers have considered necessary for the proper discharge of the responsibilities of the Cro-wn. It is the fact of' this great new nation coming forward, with all its measureless strength and possibility to testify to the enduring life of the British Empire that has already produced an impression throughout the world of more value than many ' dreadnought ' ships, an impression which throughout the world conduces both to the safety of this country and to the peace of nations.
I shall lay this ' Hansard ' on the table of the House in order that what I have read may be checked by any hon. gentleman who so desires. At page 74 of the British ' Hansard '-and this refers to the argument that was advanced that Britain was not in a position to build expeditiously the three -additional ships-at page 74 of the British ' Hansard ' of Monday, March 31, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill says:
I hope, therefore, it will be understood that there is no difficulty, either in accelerating our own ships if necessary, or in placing contracts for the construction of these Canadian, ships which are now under discussion in Canada. This can all be done without any interruption, either of our existing building programme or of the construction of foreign vessels now constructing in our yards.
I said upon rising that it was not the intention to add anything to the arguments I advanced on the last occasion this. section was under discussion in Committee. I rose merely for the purpose of confirming the statements which I then made-and which were challenged by my hon.. friend from Red Deer, in order that it may. appear on the records that what I stated' on that occasion, both in the afternoon and in the evening, was in accordance with the facts.

I have listened with considerable interest to the Minister of Finance, but really whether the Right Hon. Mr. Churchill used the words-

he attributed to him or whether he did not, does not in any way, to my mind, affect the situation as it exists at present in	Canada.
The issue between the two parties in this Parliament and throughout the country is not whether England needs these ships, or whether or not these ships should be built. We on this, side of the House agree with hon. gentlemen opposite that Canada should take her place as one of the dominant dominions of the Empire in the naval defence of the Empire. We on this side of the House are equally willing with hon. gentlemen to vote this amount of money which is suggested, or any other amount of money which may be necessary in aid of the naval defences of the British Empire. We say that Canada, as a self-governing dominion, within the Empire, rising to the state of nationhood, should herself establish a navy within her own borders manned by her own men, maintained by her own Parliament, to aid in the Empire's naval defence, and floating in the waters surrounding this dominion. Now,_ there has been, perhaps, enough said in reference to the building of these ships in Canada. 1 think it is pretty generally conceded throughout Canada that we are commercially capable and capable from the point of view of intelligence and skill, of building ships, if not perhaps, dreadnoughts^ at the present moment, at least ships which are equally as valuable to the British navy as dreadnoughts are. For, hon. gentlemen opposite must remember that the British navy is not made up of dreadnoughts only. The British Admiralty is building continually a class of cruisers which may be built in Canada just as well as in the United Kingdom, which cruisers are equally valuable with dreadnoughts as aids to the British navy.	,	.
Now, Sir, there is another question m regard to this matter which has not yet been dealt with to a great extent since this Bill came into committee. It was dwelt upon to some extent when the resolution was under discussion and on the second reading of the Bill, hut it has not been much discussed in committee. I refer to the manner in which this money is to be expended. The Government proposes that Parliament should vote $35,000,000, handing it over to the Government to be used in the aid of the naval forces of the Empire. There is nothing in the Bill which states how that money is to be expended. Hon. gentlemen opposite, the right hon. Prime Minister and others, have said that they will build three dreadnoughts. But there is nothing in the Bill -which provides for the building of three dreadnoughts. It is suggested that these ships will be built. But we are to hand that money over to the
Government to do as they please with, and after the money is placed in the hands of the Government, Parliament is absolutely debarred from any consideration as to the manner of its expenditure. If the Minister of Railways and Canals were to come down to Parliament this session and say: It is estimated that the new Welland ship canal will cost for construction about $45,000,000, and the work will take about five years to complete; I would like Parliament to vote that amount of money for that purpose; is there any hon. gentleman within the sound of my voice wlho would say that Parliament should vote that money for the minister to use as he saw fit in building that canal? It would never be thought of. Hon. gentlemen opposite would not support such a proposition. This year the minister says that $2,000,000 is about all that he will spend during the present fiscal year, and consequently he proposes a vote of that amount toward the construction of the canal. Next year, when Parliament meets, that money having been expended-and the expenditure is subjected to the investigation of the Public Accounts Committee- if the money has been properly and judiciously spent. Parliament will be prepared to vote a further sum to be handed over to the minister for the continuance of the good work for another year. That is the way parliamentary government in Canada has always been carried on, ever since the Family (Compact was broken in 1837. The fact that in those days the Governor in Couneil provided for and managed the people's money without the people's approval and without the people's concurrence was the cause of a rebellion in this country. That was the cause, and the only cause, of the rebellion of 1837 in Upper and Lower Canada, the Governor in Council endeavouring to control the affairs of this country to the extent of spending the people's money without the people's representatives having a voice in that expenditure. Sir, we thought those days were ended; we thought that the foundation stones of responsible government had been planted so deep in this country that no one would attempt to move them. But we are coming back to the same thing again. What does this Bill provide for? To place in the hands of the Governor in Council $35,000,000 to spend at their own free will, without Parliament having a word to say about itj. Sir, that is not in accordance with Liberal, views, it is not in accordance with respon-i sible government as understood in this country. And I say that is one of the questions which are vital questions in this instance; and so far as I am concerned, that is one of the questions that interests me more than the expenditure of the money and more than the building of the dreadnoughts. So far as I am concerned, I am
Mr. GERMAN.

quite prepared to join hon. gentlemen opposite in the expenditure of $35,000,000 to build dreadnoughts, but we will build these dreadnoughts under the control of Parliament, Parliament directing the expenditure of the money. We have at this moment on the statute books of Canada an Act called 1 The Naval Service Act/ and I ask the right hon. the leader of the Government if he cannot under that Act, with the approval of Parliament, do everything he is asking us to do under this Naval Aid Act? I have prepared three questions which I propose to ask my right hon. friend. The first question is, can Parliament under the Naval Service Act appropriate $35,000,000 or any other sum for the construction and equipment of battleships or armoured cruisers of the most modern and powerful type for the purpose of immediately increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire ? I ask my right hon. friend if under the Naval Service Act this Parliament has not the power to appropriate $35,000,000 or any other sum for the construction of dreadnoughts ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
proceed to propound his various questions, it will be much more convenient to answer them afterwards.

I apprehend that there
can be only one answer to the question. Can we not, under the Naval Service Act of Canada as it exists at this moment, appropriate $35,000,000-
What do you think ?

I think we certainly can. If the hon. Minister of the Naval Service had' asked Parliament, under the provisions of the Naval Service Act, to appropriate $35,000,000 for the construction of battleships-which he had a perfect right to do- Parliament could have appropriated that amount of money, or a lesser or greater sum. I want it to be distinctly understood that the matter we are discussing is not whether or not Canada shall aid Britain; we are all agreed in that. The question is how shall it be done. Shall it be done by the Governor in Council, or by the Parliament representing the people of Canada ? The second question I would ask is this: Can the Government, under the Naval Service Act, with the approval of Parliament construct or have constructed, such battleships or armoured cruisers in Great Britain, in Canada or elsewhere ? There is nothing in the present Naval Service Act to prevent the Government, if Parliament votes the money, from having these ships built in Great Britain. The late Government advertised for tenders for the construction of these ships in Canada; there was nothing to prevent them from having the ships built in the Old Country, and there
is nothing to prevent this Government from having the ships built in England if the Parliament of Canada should appropriate the money for that purpose. Third, can the Government, under the Naval Service Act, with the approval of Parliament, place such battleships or armoured cruisers, when so constructed and equipped, at the disposal of the British Admiralty ? No one can deny that, under the present Naval Service Act as it stands on the statute-books of Canada, this can be done. We can vote the money, we can build the ships, and we can place them at the disposal of the British Admiralty under such terms and conditions as Parliament shall approve. Why, then, the necessity for the Naval Aid Act ? If under the Naval Service Act you can do everything that is contemplated by the proposed Naval Aid Act, why introduce the Naval Aid Bill ? That absolutely passes my comprehension; I do not know that anyone has suggested an explanation of it, and before this Bill goes through committee- at any rate until I am gagged-I intend to insist on getting an answer to that question. We must have an explanation from the right hon. Prime Minister as to why he is endeavouring to force through this Parliament an Act to be placed on the statute-book side by side with an Act under which he can do everything contemplated in the present Bill. There must be some reason for this; my right hon. friend is too astute a lawyer not to know that, under the Act as it stands, he can do what he proposes to do under the Naval Aid Act. Why is he introducing this Bill? I hope he will tell us, but I fear he will not. My right hon. friend has been charged in this House-and he has not yet denied it-with having entered into a positive agreement with the Nationalists of Quebec to repeal the Naval Service Act. If he does not give us some reason why he is endeavouring to force this Bill through Parliament, we will have to believe, and the people of Canada will believe, that he has made such an agreement with Mr. Bourassa and his Nationalist friends. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to find out what the opinion of the people in the province of Ontario is, let them dissolve this Parliament; they will get their answer, sharp and decisive, and it will not be an answer altogether pleasing to them. We say that the reason why this Government is endeavouring to force this Bill through Parliament is because the Prime Minister has entered into an agreement with the Nationalists of the province of Quebec that he will repeal the Naval Service Act. He feels bound to do something in aid of the naval defence of the Empire, he so eloquently and intelligently, so strongly and emphatically supported that proposition in

1910 that he must now do something in aid of naval defence.	Consequently he
brings in a Bill under which when it becomes law, the Governor in Council shall control the expenditure of the money, shall control the ships after they are constructed, and shall place them in charge of the British Admiralty under such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may agree.
Is the hon. gentleman willing to vote for the appropriation of $35,000,000 for the purchase of three ships, as is proposed under the Bill now before the House?

My hon. friend is, I am sure, not so obtuse as he endeavours to show himself to be. I am certainly not willing to vote for the expenditure of $35,000,000 under the proposed legislation now under consideration, but I may tell my hon. friend that I will vote for the expenditure of such amount of money as may be considered sufficient to build dreadnoughts under the Naval Service Act as it stands on the statute books of this country at the present moment, and so will every other member on this side of the House. Let them drop their Bill, let them drop their Naval Aid Act, iniquitous as it is, and let the Minister of Marine bring down to Parliament an appropriation for the construction of - battleships and then he will see whether or not the two sides of the House can get together and get together right quickly. These hon. gentlemen talk about unanimity. It would be an excellent thing to have unanimity, it would be a grand object lesson to the nations of the world if this great Parliament of Canada could join together and stand up unanimously and say: We will vote $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 in aid of the naval defence of the Em'pire. 'Sir, that would be a grand object lesson to the nations of the world, and that, Sir, we are prepared to do, but we are prepared to do it under the control of Parliament and not under the control of the- Governor in Council.

Is my hon. friend of
opinion that, under the Naval Service Act of 1910, we could spend $100,000,000 to improve the naval forces of the Empire?

I am of the opinion that we could spend $100,000,000 or any other sum. It is for Parliament to say how much money we would spend, absolutely, that is our position. Under our policy Parliament will appropriate the money, the Government will have control of the expenditure of the money and Parliament will have control of the ships after they are built.
Mr. GERMAN.
