speechtext: House again in Committee on Bill No. 21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire.-Mr. Borden. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

When the committee
rose at six o'clock, I was dealing with the proposition that there should be no expenditure of public money in Canada except under parliamentary control and parliamentary supervision. This afternoon the hon. the Minister of Finance referred to the remarks made by the Right Hon. Winston Churchill as to the need of Canada supplying Great Britain with ships. I said then, as I say now, that whatever Mr. Churchill may have said in that regard has nothing to do with the issue as it stands to-day between the parties in Canada. I apprehend that the remarks of Mr. Churchill were made not in the spirit of necessity. If he made them at all,-and I do not intend to deny that they were made, he made them, not from the point of view of necessity but from the point of view that there was a need of unanimity. He was referring to the spectacular proposition that Canada should aid the Empire in naval defence and pointing out that that need existed. I tell hon. gentlemen opposite that in my opinion that need does exist. In that view I agree with Mr. Churchill. A need exists that all parts of the British Empire should unite in a policy of naval defence, and Canada being the brightest gem in the British Empire should be the first to make the move in aiding Great Britain in the naval defence of the Empire. With that I agree, and I believe that every hon. gentleman on this side of the House, as well as every hon gentleman on the other side, agrees with that. As I said before dinner, it is not a question of the desire to aid; it is a question as to how we should aid.	*
The bottom principle in the province of Ontario, in the old province of Upper Canada, was responsible government and parliamentary control over public expenditure That was one of the things that brought about Confederation, that and representa-

tion by population. For that principle, Mackenzie, Baldwin, George Brown, coupled with Papineau, Lafontaine and Dorion, fought for years. That is the principle which is dominant to-day in Canada, and that principle cannot be subverted and overthrown. But that principle this Government is endeavouring to subvert and overturn. The first attempt in that direction after Confederation was made in the province of Ontario in 1870, by John Sandfield Macdonald, he being then Prime Minister in a coalition government in that province. He moved and put through the legislature an Act appropriating $1,500,000 in aid of railways, and placing that money in the hands of the ministers of the Crown to be expended by Order in Council without reference to the legislature. The Hon. Edward Blake was leader of the opposition at that time, and he took issue with that policy as being subversive of all Liberal principles from time immemorial. An election was fought on that principle in Ontario m 1871 and the John Sandfield Macdonald's Government was defeated. That issue, we thought, was laid aside and that it would not rise again. What aid we find? 'Last session the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) introduced the Highways Bill. The Bill was absolutely perfect in itself excepting clause 6, which stated that the Governor in Council could spend the money provided for at his own sweet will wherever he liked to spend it. That was the clause which the Senate threw out and that is the clause which embodies exactly the principle which is embodied in this Nava] Aid Bill to-day. The Minister of Railways has reintroduced that Bill with that clause in it, and I may tell hon. gentlemen opposite, and we might as well understand where the issue lies and in what it consists, that he cannot get that Bill through Parliament so long as Liberal instincts dominate. This Bill of the right hon. Prime Minister cannot pass this Parliament so long as Liberal instincts dominate Parliament, whether it may be in the Senate or whether it may he in the House of Commons. Liberals in Canada will not stand to hand over to the Government, whether it be Liberal or Conservative, any sum of money to be expended at the will of the Governor-in-Council without the inspection and supervision of Parliament. There, it seems to me, is the clear-cut issue between the two parties on this ' question. The right hon. leader of the Government has twitted us and has said on several occasions:	You have voted to appropriate
$35,000,000. So we have, and we intend to vote for it again. I intend to ask, in the amendment which I propose to move, that the right hon. gentleman shall also vote for it and that he shall vote for it with
the rider that the money shall be expended under the approval of Parliament. If we do that we can all get together under one flag. As the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) says we will all run together like the horses of the sun, but we will run together under the Liberal flag of parliamentary control of public expenditure. When we have adopted that principle we will all be together. The amendment which I propose to move is:
That clause 2 be struck out and that the following he substituted therefor: Upon appropriations in that behalf being from time to time made by Parliament, there may be paid and applied from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of speedily increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.
I have used the word ' speedily ' instead of ' immediately ' because the word ' speedily ' was coined by the right hon. Prime Minister himself. He insisted that the word ' speedily ' should be put in the resolution of 1909; so, in deference to his superior wisdom and knowledge in that particular, I use the word ' speedily ' in this amendment which I propose. But the crux of this amendment is in these words [DOT] upon appropriations in that behalf from time to time made by Parliament.' This Opposition will vote all the money that is necessary to maintain the supremacy of Great Britain and tc ensure that the white ensign shall float the seas supreme. I will for one; I will give you $35,000,000, or $100,000,000 if you need it, or if Great Britain wants it. So will every hon. member on this side of the House. There is no difference of opinion in so far as that part of it is concerned. I am saying that simply as an illustration of our idea of what may be necessary. We know full well that it is not necessary. My right hon. friend said there was an emergency. The emergency is a long time coming. Wherein does it exist? Great Britain is perfectly capable of taking care of herself. She is as supreme to-day as she always was and she will remain supreme for years to come. Speaking for myself, what I would like to see would be the Government of Canada appropriating a liberal amount of money for building ships. Perhaps the first ones might neces" sarily be built in England, although I do not know about that. We can build them here, but at all events, I would like to see Canada building ships and manning them with our own young Canadians.
You never can build up a Canadian navy until you begin. Hon. gentlemen opposite had the nucleus of one when they came into power. They had the naval college established with our own young men attending there. Some of them are in

England now, and I am happy to say that they are standing right up to the mark with
all the English cadets at the naval college there. Have your naval college here, have your training ships here and build up the nucleus of a navy. Begin now. Why delay? If you ever intend to have one why not begin now? You might as well begin now as ten years from now. You will be no better off ten years from now than you are today. Then, I repeat, begin now. Vote the money, build the ships, establish your naval college, provide your training ships, start in as a nation intending to support the British Empire. You will do more in aid of the British Empire by doing that than you will by sending $35,000,000 over to England.
Everyone knows that England does not need the money. That is too -selbevident to be discussed. The right non. Prime Minister said that the Government of England want $35,000,000 to help them in building battleships. They would say: All right, we will take it if you like, but we do not need it and we do not want it. Everyone knows they do not want $35,000,000; what they want is the sentiment in Canada which is behind the $35,000,000.
Hear, hear.
That is what they want,
That is what they are going to get.
Hear, hear.
I am glad to hear hon. gentlemen opposite cheer that. They want the sentiment behind the money.
They will get it.
They will get it in this way: if you hon. gentlemen on the other side will simply drop this idiotic Bill and say: under the Canadian Naval Service Act we will vote $35,000,000 and build ships-
Why do you not vote it?

You have on your statute books at the present time an Act which allows you to get the money. You want this legislation simply because you want to control the money by Order in Council instead of by Parliament. You say it shall be done by Order in Council and we say it shall be done with the approval of [DOT]Parliament. Let any man opposite challenge that statement if he can, we are absolutely behind a rock of impregnability in that. The Prime Minister has got the ability of any hon. member in this House.
Hear, hear.

Yes, he has the ability of any man in this House, and let him Mr. GERMAN.
get up if he can and challenge my statement as to the distinction between the Naval Service Act and the Naval Aid Act. There is no difference between the two except that the Naval Aid Act says that this money shall be spent by the Governor in Council and that the ships shall be under the control of the Governor in Council and handed over to the British Admiralty on such arrangement as the Governor in Council may make, whereas the Naval Service Act says that the money shall be expended under the control of Parliament. We will vote any money needed to aid the British Empire; we will give our life-blood for the Empire; we will stand by the British Empire very much longer than the blatant gentlemen on the other side of the House who shout loyalty and do nothing. I beg leave to move as an amendment to the amendment already before the House:
That clause 2 of the Bill be struck out and the following substituted therefor:	_
On appropriations in that behalf being from to time made by Parliament, there may be paid and applied from and out of 'the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of speedily increasing the effective, naval forces of the Empire.
Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (St. John City): I do not intend to inflict a speech upon the committee just at present, but I want to correct a statement which the Minister of Marine made as to the cost of building battleships in the United States as compared with the cost of building them in England. The object the Minister of Marine had in view was to convince the people of the country that it would cost a vastly larger sum of money to build war vessels in Canada than it would cost to build them in England.

I rise to a point of
order. Is the hon. gentleman speaking on the amendment to the amendment?

If my hon. friend will listen he will be able to judge for himself. The argument of the Minister of Marine was along the line taken by the Prime Minister that it would be the height of folly for Canada to undertake to build war vessels in this country, to attempt to create shipyards and a shipbuilding industry here, when at vastly less cost the vessels could be secured in England. The hon. gentleman sought to leave the impression that the battleship Pennsylvania was going to cost the Government of the United States $17,000,000. I quote from the Scientific American of the 15th of March, 1913, and I think every hon. member will agree that among the many able journal^ in America none is more reliable and to be depended on in scientific matters than is the Scientific American. The article states:	.	-j- t'Mi
[DOT]9149

Bids for building the Pennsylvania-Of the, three best bids for the construction of our latest battleship, the Pennsylvania (the largest ship authorized or1 under construction), made by the (Newport News, the New York Shipbuilding and the Pore River Company, that of the Newport News yard of $7,255,900 was the lowest and the contract has gone to that firm. The total cost of the ship when completed, with guns, armour and equipment, will be $14,172,000. The Pennsylvania was described in a recent issue in which her dimensions were given as 600 feet between perpendiculars, 625 feet over all, 397 feet beam and draught 29 feet. The maximum full load displacement will be 32,500 tons. She will be the largest, best protected and most powerful ship afloat on the day of her launching.
Those are statements which I believe can be absolutely relied upon. As I under-' stand it the vessel of the super-dreadnought type which this Government proposes to have built in England, is to have a displacement of 28,000 tons in stead of the 32,500 tons o,f the Pennsylvania. And the figure given by the Prime Minister as to the cost which this Government expected to pay for the building of sudh a vessel in England, if I remember rightly, was $13,500,000 or $13,700,000. I give the figures from memory, but I think I am near the mark. Now, we have here the warship Pennsylvania of 4,500 tons greater displacement which will be constructed at the shipyards of Newport News at a cost, completely equipped, with armour-plate guns, everything necessary in order to start the warship afloat, of $14,172,000, a difference of something less than seven per cent as compared with the cost of the cheaper war-vessel to he built in England. This, I think, will establish the statement which I have made and for which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House contend generally, that if we go forward with courage, with a courage which will be worthy of the Canadian nation, we shall be able to establish in the very near future shipyards in Canada upon the Atlantic and the Pacific, where all the war vessels which will he required for the Canadian navy, and which will be able to take their part in defending onr coasts and also in defending the Empire, can -be built within a very few years at a very little greater expenditure than will be paid out by the Government if these ships are built in England. At the same time, we should be creating a great ship-building industry in this country, we should give employment to Canadian labour, and we shall do something worthy of our Canadian people and in which our Canadian nation will take a just pride.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Like my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) I have no intention at all of inflicting a speech upon the House. And I should not have
spoken at all at this stage had not it been that the hon. gentleman has attempted, and unfortunately for himself with very little success, to throw doubt upon the figures which I gave to the House with regard to the cost of the battleship Pennsylvania now -being constructed by the Government of the United States. But before I take up that subject, I desire to refer to another. The hon. gentleman has dwelt, time and time and time again in the course of the one hundred and one speeches which he has made on this subject in this House, upon the wonderful success of what he calls the Fore River Shipbuilding Company of the United States, which he visited and which he has held forth to this House, time and time again, and over and over again, as a notable example of the speed at comparatively small cost with which a successful ship-building company could be built up in the United States, and by inference, according to his reasoning, could be built up in Canada. Listening to the hon. gentleman's remarks as I have done time and time again, one would be led to believe that the Fore River Shipbuilding Company -was one of the most successful enterprises of modem time. Can hon. gentlemen who listened to the eulogies which the hon. member -for St. John spoke upon this great company believe that that company which he has held up to the admiration of the House as the acme of perfection in everything in ship-building has actually gone into liquidation? In case any hon. gentleman may have any doubt on that score, I wish to read some extracts from a magazine known as Shipping Illustrated, published in New York and from the issue of that paper of May 3:
The sale of the Fore River Shipbuilding Company to the Bethlehem Steel Company is the solution of a problem which had for some time been puzzling the wiseacres among the shipping and shipbuilding trades,

Among them, I suppose, is to be enumerated my hon. friend.
-who wondered how long the first-named concern would be able to hold out without financial reorganization in -the face of the losses which it was known to have sustained in connection with recent contracts for commercial work, not to mention the two Argentine battleships, Rivdavia and Moreno, originally intended to be delivered in the middle of the year, and which are still lying at the fitting-out wharfs in Quincy, Mass., and Camden, N.J.
The House will remember how the hon. gentleman told us about this company having secured the contract in competition with English ship-building companies, and in competition with ship-building companies all over the world. They did secure the contract, but the result has been very disastrous, and these ships, which should have

been delivered months ago, are still lying there in an unfinished condition.
The circular addressed to the stockholders of the Fore River Company by the directors states that ' being aware that the completion of certain existing contracts -would in the near future leave the company with its working capital seriously impaired to such an extent as to necessitate financing (they) have learned with satisfaction of an arrangement made by the stockholders' committee acting on the initiative and suggestion of the directors and representing a very large proportion (over 80 per cent) of both preferred and common stock to sell property of the company to the Bethlehem Steel Company, which assumes all its obligations and takes all its assets. The ' certain existing contracts ' are well known to our readers as the two white elephants which the Fore River Company contracted to build for the Argentine Government in 1S>10. The securing of these contracts -was looked upon at the time in the lay press as a masterpiece of American diplomacy and business acumen. Naval constructors and ship-builders, however, looked upon these contracts as one of the most ill-advised steps ever taken by a large industrial concern, and now that the last instalment due before delivery has been paid by the Argentine Government, the ships being still a long way from completion, the contractors are compelled to turn over their property to the ordnance sub-contractors, the Bethlehem Steel Company, in order to save what they can of their investment before the final wrangle expected to take place when the ships have gone -through the trials.
And the editor adds:
The pitiful sequel to the flapdoodle which filled the columns of the press at the -time the Fore River Company naively assumed the contract with the Argentine Government at which the largest European naval construction firms had looked askance.
There is more, but I will not take up the time of the House to read it. I think I have read enough, however, to show the House that the foundation the hon. gentleman so elaborately built up with regard to the ease with which ship-building yards could be provided in Canada by the example of the Fore River Shipbuilding Company	of	Quincy, Massachusetts, has
crumbled as the result of the deplorable financial condition in which that company finds itself at the present time. My hon. friend says he did not rise for the purpose of making a speech; it was very kind of my hon. friend to be so self-denying in that respect. He said he rose only for the purpose of showing how incorrect-that, if not the actual word, was what he said in substance-were the figures I quoted to this House as to the cost of building the battleship Pennsylvania in the United States. The figures I gave to the House on that occasion I desire to give again, and I wish to say that those figures were correct then, and, as I repeat them to the House now, they Mr. HAZEN.
are absolutely correct. My figures were taken from the official records of the United States as to the estimated cost of the ships per ton, as shown by the proceedings of the Committee on Naval Affairs on January 3, 1913. They were submitted to the Committee on Naval Affairs by Admiral Knut, the chief director of the United States navy. If my figures are wrong, then the official figures laid before the Committee on Naval Affairs of the Congress of the United States are wrong, and I do not think that was the ease. I mentioned the battleship Pennsylvania, of approximately 31,000 tons. I said that the total estimated cost of that ship, according to those figures, built in a navy yard- which in the United States is considered to result in a superior form of construction, was $16,345,275. If my hon. friend will refer to page 348 of that return, he will find that the estimated returns regarding the battleship Pennsylvania are presented according to the figures I have quoted. I also gave other figures to the House; I said that if the ship were built according to an eight-hour day schedule, the cost would be $15,043,803, the figures in detail being: construction and maintenance, $7,800,000; equipment, $110,000; armour and armament, $7,133,803, a total cf $15,043,803. If built in one of the navy-yards of the United States, in which it is claimed that the vessels built are of better construction than those built by contract, the cost would be as follows: construction and maintenance, $9,750,000, equipment, $110,000; armour and armament, $6,485,275, a total of $16,345,275, or an estimated cost of $527 per ton. At the same time I gave figures with regard to a battle cruiser, but as my hon. friend has not referred to them, it will not be necessary for me to deal with them at the present time. I have here a letter from a prominent official at Washington-whose -name I cannot now disclose, but I may have the privilege of giving it later-in which he says:
On page 348 of the enclosed you will find the estimated cost of the battleship Pennsylvania of approximately 30,000 tons. She is now being built in the Newport News yard of a private firm, and the estimate given, namely, $15,013,803, was based on the actual bids made. The actual cost will be somewhat higher than the estimate, though of course the actual figures cannot be yet known. Between $15,000,000 and $16,000,000 is the statement given to me by the department. You will notice that the Government now require their ships to be built under regulations providing for an eight hours' day.
These were the figures which I gave to the House; any hon. gentleman can verify them by turning up the records of the United States Congress. In view of that fact, I am not disposed to admit for one single moment that I made the slightest error in the figures that I laid before the

House on the occasion to which I have referred.
In the recent debate on this matter, an expression was made use of by my hon. friend, which will be seen in the Commons Debates of March 3, 1913, to the effect that it is mere moonshine-I think that was the language of the hon. gentleman-to talk about a shipbuilding plant costing huge sums of money, and that as a matter of fact the Newport News Company's yard, which is said to be capable of constructing any dreadnought, cost approximately $4,000,000.
Mr. PUGSLEY. My hon. friend is wrong; it was the Fore River shipbuilding yard to which I referred. I visited this yard myself, I saw the work, and I obtained the information as to its cost from the president of the company.

In other fwords the plant that had cost the Fore River Company $3,800,000. is purchased by the Bethlehem Company for $4,800,000:	That
does not look much like a bankrupt concern. It does not look like a company being obliged to go out of business. Let me read what the New York Times says, and place it against the statement my hon. friend read.
Fore River Yards Bought by Schwab-Bethlehem Steel Company Acquires $1,800,000 Shipbuilding Plant at Quincy, Mass.-New Line in Big System-Corporation will Compete with Entire World in Construction of War vessels.
Special to the New York Times.
Bethlehem April 25.-The Bethlehem Steel Company, directed by Charles M. Schwab, has bought the Fore River Shipbuilding Company, a $4,800,000 corporation, at Quincy, Mass., and will enter into competition with the world in building battleships.
It does not look much like a bankrupt concern, when they are going to enter into competition with the world in the building of battleships.
Will the hon. member read the part in which he says it has been bought for $4,800,000?

It is in the heading.
Fore River Yards Bought by Schwab, Bethlehem Steel Company Acquires $4,800,000, Shipbuilding Plant at Quincy, Mass.
It goes on:
The purchase of the Fore river yards completes an organization with 25,000 men on its payroll, and with ability to build and equip a modern battleship from keelplate to armoured turrets.
According to the Bethlehem Company's management, the purchase of the Fore river plant was to complete the development of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation into an organization capable of turning out all iron and steel products used on land and sea.
Contrary to rumour, this latest act of enlargement is not aimed at the Steel Trust, nor does it mean war with any of the other shipyards. It merely places the Bethlehem interests in a position to bid in competition with all the w-orld for the warship business.

The Fore river plant has the contract for one of the Argentine battleships. The contract for another went to the New York Shipbuilding Company at Camden. Mr. Schwab has the contract to furnish steel armour, guns, and ammunition for both vessels. This deal gave him a new insight to shipbuilding, and to perfect an organization he felt he needed the Fore river yard.
And yet my hon. friend has sought to convey the impression that it was a bankrupt company. Let me read further:
Boston April 25.-The transfer of the Fore river shipyard is expected to double the ship building at this port. The company has transacted an annual business of $6,000,000 to $12,000,000.
Twenty-three vessels are in course of construction at the yard, involving contracts amounting to $20,000,000 .
And that is supposed to be a bankrupt concern.
Practically all the vessels are war vessels. The company is building a battleship, nine submarines, two destroyers, and a tender for the United States. In addition there is under construction a monster battleship for the Argentine republic. Schwab interests intend adding a large dry dock to the yard's equipment.
The Fore River Shipbuilding Company's officers are Rear Admiral Francis T. Bowles, retired, president, and .F. C. Dumaine, vice president.	.

May I ask my hon.
friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether Cammell, Laird and Company's
tender was not a tender to build these vessels at the port of St. John?
Why did you not accept it?

The reason was that in the province of Quebec the question of a Canadian navy was being made an issue. It was not being made an issue in any other part of Canada, it is true, but in the province of Quebec it was being made an issue. In that province there were certain public men going from platform to platform seeking to create a prejudice against the Government, seeking to make the people believe that in some way the creation of a Canadian navy would work disastrously to the people of Quebec, that it would mean conscription and that it would mean that the young men of Quebec would be drawn off into foreign wars. I need not repeat to you, Mr. Chairman, the statements which were made in Quebec. You know them, Sir, all too well. You know the unworthy appeals that were made to prejudices in that province.
The Government thought that under the circumstances, as only a very short time had elapsed from the return of the then Prime Minister and the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries from England before the dissolution took place, that it would be proper to leave the awarding of contracts for the building of war vessels and to start upon the construction of the Canadian navy until after the elections took place. Then, after the elections took place, it was thought that it would not be right to award the contract, but that it should be left for the incoming Government to deal with it. The late Government did not deal in an exceptional manner with the case in respect to the building of war vessels, and in proof of that all I have to say is that, in respect to a very large contract at the port of St. John, the contract for the development of Courtenay bay, which ran into an expenditure of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000, tenders had been called. I would have been very glad to have seen that contract let because it meant so much to my own city and to the province of New Brunswick, but the Government felt that in view of the elections it was proper to leave that contract for the incoming Government to deal with. I was glad that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, with what little assistance I was able to give him- and it was of some avail-induced his colleagues to award the contract for these great harbour works at Courtenay bay.
But here my hon. friend fell down, and fell down in the most deplorable manner. Because of the alliance which I have described outside of this House, and which 1 will continue to describe upon every reasonable opportunity which comes to me, as the unholy alliance with the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec, he was



obliged to return that deposit of $100,000 to Cammell, Laird and Company, and he was obliged not to take any action upon the tenders and to abandon, for the time being at all events, the idea of a Canadian navy. My hon. friend has heard the question ot the hon. member for Algorna (Mr. Boyce) as to where Cammell, Laird and Company proposed to build. I will ask my hon. friend; as the honourable man that I know him to be, to tell this House where Cammell, Laird and Company proposed, by their written tender, to build these war vessels. I will ask him if it is not true that, when he came into office, he found there the tender of Cammell, Laird and Company with a deposit of $100,000, and no other deposits because they had all been returned to the tenderers, and I will ask him particularly where Cammell, Laird and Company proposed to build these war vessels. He knows, as I do, that they proposed to build them at St. John. He knows, as I do, that they had selected a site for their shipyard right alongside of the dry-dock which is being constructed in Courtenay bay, and he knows as well as I do that, if he had induced his colleagues to let the contract to Cammell, Laird and Company, long before this the shipyards would have been well equipped, the keels of a number of these vessels would have been laid and there would have been a good many men employed in the shipyard at the port of St. John.
I mention this because it is due to the Minister of Marine that he should tell the House what the tender of Cammell, Laird and Company was, what vessels they proposed to build, what were the prices they asked, and where they proposed to establish their shipyard. And, as to the cost of constructing a shipyard being so great as to be beyond the financial ability of the people of Canada, how about the great firm of Vickers, Son and Maxim? Under an inducement offered by the late Government they constructed a great floating dry-dock in England, they brought it to the port of Montreal, they are establishing a shipyard there, and I have it upon authority, the accuracy of which I cannot question, that Vickers, Son and Maxim offered to this Government to build battleships in Montreal and offered further that, within eighteen months of the day the contract would be given them, they would lay the keel of a battleship in the yard they are constructing in Montreal. Does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries deny that? I have risked for the correspondence to be brought down, and the answer of the Prime Minister was that the correspondence was of a secret character and Vickers, Son and Maxim declined to allow it to be brought before Parliament. Vickers, Son and Maxim have great shipyards in the United Kingdom and if a contract is given for three great battleships to be built in Mr PUGSLEY.
the United Kingdom, I venture to say that Vickers, Son and Maxim will be bidders for the building of these ships there. It makes no difference to them whether they build at Montreal or in the United Kingdom. I can well understand thev would not wish to do anything that would create a feeling of antagonism as between them and the present Government which is determined to build not in Canada but in the United Kingdom; determined not to spend this $35,000,000 by employing Canadian labour, but to send it out of the country in order to give employment to the labouring people of the United Kingdom. I have it on authority;
I do not mind giving my authority, I did not get the information in confidence and I will give the authority to this House for the statement I have made. Before I do so let me say that all, or a large portion of the negotiations which took place with regard to the buildi.ng of a dry-dock and the creation of a ship-building plant at the port of Montreal, took place between the late Government and the late Board of Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, and one of these harbour commissioners was Mr. Ballantyne, and Mr. Ballantyne is my authority. Mr Ballantyne told me that the firm of Vickers, Son and Maxim had offered to build battleships at their yard in Montreal and stated that if they got the contract, they would be able, within eighteen months, to lay the keel of the first battleship. It would be interesting to this House and to this country, if we had this secret and confidential correspondence which has taken place. I am sorry we have not got it; I do not know what it contains but I have given the statement made to me, not in a confidential manner but in the ordinary way of conversation, by a gentleman who had much to do with the negotiations for the building of the dry-dock and ship-building plant at Montreal, and upon that I assert with the utmost confidence that the firm of Vickers, Son and Maxim, if the contract were given to them for building war vessels at Montreal, would be quite prepared to go ahead and within eighteen months to lay the keel of the first battleship. I am very sorry to have taken up so much of the time of the committee, and I would not have done so had it not been that my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) made the remarks he did. I am sorry, sorry beyond measure, that my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) should he straining every nerve to present arguments to the people of Canada against encouraging the building of war vessels in this country. I am sorry that he should be endeavouring by hook or by crook to show to this House that it would be infinitely better, instead of seeking to build war vessels in Canada, to postpone for

all -time the ship-building industry in this country, and to hand over now our money to the British authorities to have these vessels built in England. I hardly expected that from my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen), who boasted that the smell of the salt water was in his nostrils and who gloried in the memory of the old days when St. John was one of the great shipbuilding ports of the world; when St. John turned out those splendid ships which sailed in every ocean and which were the pride, not only of St. John, but of the Maritime provinces. I am pained beyond measure that my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) wh.o claimed he would like to see shipbuilding revived in this country, has so little faith in the intelligence, enterprise and ability of the Canadian people and Canadian workmen, that he would send this money out of the country instead of employing it in the ship-building industry here. I am sorry it falls to his lot, as Minister of Marine and Fisheries (an office which gives him the initiative with regard to the building of the ships), that he, the representative of the great constituency _ of St. John should strike the blow which he has struck, not only at his own constituency but at the entire Dommion. Let me ask my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) if it is not a terrible price to pay for that alliance between the Conservative party and the Nationalist party of Quebec ?

My hon. friend has seen fit to discuss many other matters. He is obessed with the idea that he can get some political advantage by repeating the statement that the Government of which I am Minister of Marine and Fisheries and Minister ol Naval Affairs did not enter into a contract with Oammell, Laird and Company for the construction of the cruisers and torpedo destroyers for which tenders were asked by the late Government, and for which tenders were received five months before the late Government went out of power. The hon. gentleman may take all the satisfaction he can get from my conduct in that regard, but I would tell him that either before the people of my own constituency or before the people of Canada I am prepared to stand face to face with my hon. friend on any occasion and to prove to any man who' is not influenced by partisan feelings or party passions that the course taken by the Government and by myself as Minister of Marine and Fisheries was in the public interest and in the interests of this country. The hon. gentleman tells the people that this contract should ' have been entered into, and, had it been entered into, that these ships would have been built at St. John. I pointed out to my hon. friend, and I have never received a satisfactory answer from him, that those tenders were received on the 1st day of May, and that the Government of which my hon, friend was a member remained in office until October 10, a period of oyer five months after those tenders were received. Where was then my hon. friend's vaunted influence? Where was his professed anxiety for the interests of the people of his constituency when he allowed those contracts during that period of time to remain in a pigeon hole in the city of Ottawa, and Shad absolutely no regard for those interests for which he now appears to be so solicitous? The hon. gentleman has referred to the contract for the work at Courtenay bay. Election after election, year in and year out the hon. gentleman has said to the people of St. John: return me to power and in a short time you will have these works going on in Courtenay bay. In the election of 1908 they were told, through the newspaper press, that if the hon. gentleman and the Government of which he was a member were returned to power, only a short time would elapse before large steamers would be seen loading and unloading at the docks in Courtenay bay. From 1908 to 1911 not a blow was struck. Tenders were called before the election, but no contract was entered into; the matter was held dangling before the eyes of the people, and it is my firm conviction that, had the hon. gentleman's Government been returned to power, the matter
would still be dangling before the eyes of the people. The hon. gentleman says the ships would have been built at St. John, but I have seen statements in the press by other hon. gentlemen to the effect that they would have been built at Sydney, and that they would have been built at Halifax. But I have a higher authority than the hon. gentleman to show that these ships would not have been built at St. John; the hon. gentleman's leader stated in most unequivocal terms in this House that these ships would be built at the port of Montreal. Let me head to this House the words of the right hon. leader of the Opposition as reported on page 1063 of ' Hansard ' of December 12, 19127
Yes; we thought as the general elections were coming, that it would not he fair, in a matter of this kind, which was at issue between the two parties, to award the contract in case there might be, as there was, a change of government. I say

The hon. gentleman was speaking with all the responsibility attaching to him as an ex-prime minister of this country

I say now that the Governmeni in power would have been better advised if they had awarded the contracts, and, had they done so, we would at the present time have under construction on the stocks in Montreal four cruisers and six destroyers.
He does not even suggest that any of these ships would be built at St. John. The contracts called for four cruisers and six destroyers, and we have the positive statement of the hon. gentleman's leader, which I am sure he will not repudiate, that, if the contract had been entered into, these four cruisers and six destroyers would be under construction on the stocks at Montreal. The hon. gentleman can fight this matter out with his leader.
I do not propose to trespass further upon the time of the House in regard to this matter, but I say to my hon. friend, that before he again attempts to make statements to this House such as those he has made with regard to the Fore River Shipbuilding Company, and before he again intimates that any assertions I have made are not warranted by the facts, he had better be more sure of his evidence, and more sure that I have not in my hand the proof for every statement I make. It is simply a flight of the imagination of my hon. *friend. Mr. ITAZEN

My hon. friend ought
to have told us what was the alliance between the Conservative party and the Nationalist party. He has said that I have no evidence that there was that alliance. Let me tell him that the statement was made in many and many a newspaper giving speeches which were made by Nationalist candidates to the effect that they had the assurance that if the Conservative party were returned to power the Naval Act w'ould be repealed. That was the statement made upon many a platform, that was the statement made not only by Nationalists but by Conservatives in the province of Quebec, running in alliance with the Nationalist party. If the naval law had been repealed, then, of course, a Canadian navy could not be constructed because the Canadian navy was ^ to be constructed under the Canadian Naval Service Act. If you repealed the Act of course the contract for the ships would go with the repeal. That is the evidence which I have and I am sure that there are hundreds and thousands of people in the province of Quebec who could corroborate the statements I have made tonight. But my hon. friend has said that the reason the contract was not given for the building of these ten vessels was that he had concluded, upon the report of experts of his department, that these vessels would be obsolete before they were constructed. What does that mean, if it means anything? It means that Canada could never build war vessels, it means that Canada could never give a contract for a number of war vessels running over a period of six years because before the six years would expire, according to the argument of my hon. friend, these vessels would become obsolete. Is that not absurd? My hon. friend has forgotten to tell this committee that under that contract two of these vessels were to be constructed about every fourteen months, those ten ships were to be built in six years and as each vessel would be constructed it would be delivered to the Government. Would it be obsolete within fourteen months after the contract for its construction was given? What does it mean for a war vessel to become obsolete? It means that, owing to changes in designs, improvements are made and a vessel which might be regarded as up-to-date to-day would in five or six or ten years not be considered up-to-date. But under the term? of the contract as under the terms of all Government ^contracts it would be quite open to the department to change the specifications at any time before the vessel was actually placed under construction, if not at any time before the vessel would be actually completed; and, under the terms of the contract, if these changes involved any additional expenditure the Government would give an allowance to the contractors, while-

if the cost would be reduced by the change the contractor would have to make an allowance to the Government. That is the case with all contracts and it was the case in these contracts. These specifications were prepared by the British Admiralty, presumably they were the best for that class of vessel known to the experts of the Admiralty. If they could be improved upon why did not the minister ask the Admiralty to have the experts make the improvements upon them? No, Sir, if it is parliamentary for me to say so, I tell my hon. friend that he is humbugging the people of this country.

They were of the opinion that he not merely neglected the interests of the people to whom he owed a supreme duty, but that he absolutely betrayed their interests, and that was why hundreds and thousands of those who had been his admirers, ceased to follow him. The result was that, when he appealed to the electorate, he was left at home and given an opportunity to devote his great ability to his private business. My hon. friend says that when I made the statement from a newspaper report that the Bethlehem Company had bought this plant for $4,800,000 I was misleading this committee. He sought to convey the impression, whether in words or not, in a manner
which I think is unworthy of a member of this House

I do not think the
word ' unworthy ' should be applied to a member of this House.

Then I will use other
language and say that in a manner unworthy of any gentleman in this country, he sought to convey the impression that I deliberately intended to deceive this committee. I refer to the "Montreal Star, which contains a despatch from Quincy, Mass., the very seat and home of the Fore River ship-building plant. This is what the Montreal Star says:
What date ?

April 26.
Special to The Montreal Star.
Quincy, Mass., April 26.-Announcement is made to-day that the Fore River Shipbuilding Company, of which Rear Admiral Francis T. Bowles (retired), is president, has been sold to the Bethlehem Steel Company, of which Charles M. Schwab is the head.

It proceeds:
In addition, there is in construction a battleship for the Argentine Republic.
' The Schwab interests are said to have elaborate plans on foot to enlarge the Fore river plant. A monster dry dock is reported to be one of the improvements contemplated.
I repeat, Sir, that if you take the statements in the New York Times and Montreal Star, the reasonable inference is that the Bethlehem Steel Company was not purchasing the plant of the Fore River

Shipbuilding Company as a decadent industry, or as a bankrupt concern, but that they were purchasing it in OTder to enlarge their operations in order to enable them the better to compete with the whole world in the building of battleships, as the newspapers say.
I just wish to say another word or two in regard to the statement of my hon. friend that in some way I have been seeking to do him an injury in regard to his return of the deposit of the Cammell-Laird Company. I would be sorry to do my hon. friend an injury, but when I found that as - Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as the one member of the Government of all others whose voice would be potent in the awarding of the contract for the building of war vessels, that he, having before him a tender to build those ten war vessels in the harbour of St. John adjoining the dry dock which is now under construction, that he saw in his department a deposit of the sum of $100,000, and that he returned without just cause and without any reason whatever that deposit to Cammell, Laird and Company I say he did an injustice to Canada and an injustice to the city of St. John for which it is my duty to condemn him. I do so not in order to do him a personal injury, but in order to let the people of his constituency and mine know that, when he had the golden opportunity of his life to do a great thing for his people, at the beck and nod of the Nationalist party of Quebec, he threw away that opportunity and sacrificed his constituency in order to help his Government to carry out the unholy alliance which existed between the Conservative party and the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec. My hon. friend says, there cannot be anything in your argument because the right hon. the leader of the Opposition made a statement that if this Government had let the contract there would have been ten war vessels under construction at the port of Montreal. Sir, if this Government had let the contract, the leader of the Opposition would have had nothing to do with it. What voice would he have had in letting the contract? Would my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have gone to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and said, I want your consent to enter jnto this contract? Surely not. My hon. friend says that my quarrel is with the leader of the Opposition. It is not. After the late Government left .office, the leader of that Government and the members of that Government were powerless, so far as this contract was concerned. My quarrel is with the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I do not want to know, the people of St. John do not want to know, and the people of Canada do not want to know, -what the late Government would Mr. PUGSLEY.
have done if it had been returned to power. They want to know what it was the duty of the present Government to do. The present Minister of .Marine and Fisheries came into office and he found there a tender from Cammell, Laird and Company, not to build war vessels in Montreal, or at Sydney, or at Halifax, but at the port of St. John, and he found also a deposit of $100,-
000.	As I say, it was not part of his duty to come to the leader of the late Government, or to me, or to anybody else; it was his duty to look at the tender, to look at the deposit, to look at the conditions which the Cammell-Laird Company offered. Their tender was the lowest tender, and it was his duty to act upon it. He had the opportunity to do so, and he did not take it, and that is why I say that he fell down in a most deplorable manner.
I repeat, Sir, that he fell down in the most deplorable manner. Mv hon. friend says that in regard to the work in Courtenay bay, he does not believe that, if the late Government had been returned to power, that work would have gone on. . He says that in 1908 I had promised it to the people of St. John, that I had promised it again before the elections of 1911, and that, if the late Government had been returned to power, it would have been kept dangling before the eyes of the people of St. John. Is there any justification for that statement? My hon. friend talks of making stump speeches. What was he doing when he made that statement? He was making that statement not to influence the members of this House, but in the hope that in some way or other he could create a prejudice against me among the people of St. John.

You will see it in the
Standard to-morrow morning.

It will appear in headlines in the Standard tomorrow morning that the hon. gentleman had made a most eloquent and impressive speech, the greatest speech of his life-and my hon. friend can make a good speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What will we read about your speech in the Telegraph?

Ah, the Telegraph is
always accurate. But now is the charge that my hon. friend makes against me based upon reason? The development of Courtenay bay was a great work and it meant the expenditure of a good many millions of dollars. When I became Minister of Public Works in 1907 I at once took into consideration the question of improved facilities at the port of St. John, upon the west side and upon the east side. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) knows that, in view of the rapidity with which the business of

the port is growing, it will be difficult to provide the facilities that are needed to accommodate the winter business which passes through the port of St. John. I had Courtenay bay investigated. There was a great basin which was dry at low tide. The question of whether it could be developed, depended upon whether the bottom of the bay was entirely composed of a deposit of silt or whether there was rock in the bay. In order to determine the feasibility of that work it was necessary that almost every foot of that vast area should bef tested by (boring. I had engineers working at these boring operations for a considerable length of time and after that work was done we had plans carefully prepared. These plans were submitted to the Government, they were gone over, they were revised by engineers and at last the plans were approved and tenders called. The time that the tenders were called was in the early part of the summer of 1911. They could not be called before that time. It took a great deal of time and a great deal of expert examination in order to determine whether these plans could be carried out at a cost which would be reasonably within the means of the people of Canada. Although my hon friend and those associated with him-and I have evidene of this-tried to depart from the plans which we had prepared for the development of Courtenay bay, they found themselves at last obliged to let the contract hinder these plans and upon the tenders which we had called for before we went out of office. In so far as I am aware, the plans have not been altered in one single particular. The people of St. John have reason to-day to be grateful to me, and grateful to the Government of which I was a member, in that we had proceeded so vigorously and had had the plans for *this great development work so carefully prepared as that when my hon. friend came into office he was not able to alter a line in the specifications or plans. My hon. friend thought at one time of abandoning the tenders^did he not? Did he not think at one time of cutting the contract up into smaller parcels and yielding to the attacks which were made upon me before the election because I had called for one tender for this enormous work? Did not my hon. friend come to the conclusion that if he did that, and if he departed from the plans which we had had prepared, it would mean his political death in the constituency of St. John? Was it not for that reason, as much as because my hon. friend desired to promote the interests of his constituency, that he signed the contract under the plans we had prepared and under, the tenders which we had called? While I was glad
that my hon. friend went along the lines which we had laid down, and while 1 was glad to see the Government following along the path which we had mapped out for them, yet I realized that if they had not been carrying out our plans they would have had very little to do during the eighteen months in which they have been in office. While it is gratifying to know that the Government is going on with the work in connection with Courtenay bay I do repeat that it is very much to be regretted that when my hon. friend had the opportunity of following up this great work of the development of Courtenay bay bv the creation of a great ship-building yard and the establishment of a ship-building industry, he fell down so lamentably and sacrificed to such a deplorable extent the interests of Canada and the interests of the constituency which he ought to have felt it his duty to maintain and protect.

Mr. Chairman, while it
may not be very entertaining or edifying to the members of the committee to protract this discussion between my non. friend (Mr. Pugsley) and myself, I would just like to say a few words in reply. My hon. friend has^ got so in the habit of making assertions-

want it understood because we want to have the .same latitude for other members.

He has made a lot of assertions about Courtenay bay, the great majority of which have not the "lightest foundation in fact. The hon. gentleman makes the assertion that I intended to cut this contract up into small lots. As far as I am aware no consideration was ever given to any such proposal at all,, but I will tell my hon. friend that the Government awarded the contract for Courtenay bay, at a sum, of $250,000 less than the lowest tenderer, or in other words, the lowest tenderer was compelled to reduce his price by that amount. My hon. friend has referred also to what his right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said in regard to the building of these vessels at Montreal and he asks what the leader of the Government would have had to do with it.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. What I asked was, what the leader of the Opposition had to do with it.

speechtext:
I stand corrected; it was
the leader of the Opposition and the leader of the previous Government, of which any hon. friend was. so distinguished a member. He wants to know what he would have had to do with it. One would imagine that he would have had a good deal to do with it if a contract had been awarded as it should have been, if my hon. friend is right, when the Government of my right hon. friend, the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in power. We have the assertion of the leader of the Opposition that if this contract had been *entered into his six cruisers and four destroyers would have been on the stocks and under construction in the city of Montreal. Therefore, if any conclusion is to be drawn from the argument of my hon. friend, it is that there never was a possible chance of having these ships built at St. John by the Government of which my hon. friend was a member and of which the leader of the Opposition was the head. I will leave my hon. friend to work that argument out to suit himself. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley), a little nettled, has referred to the fact that he and I parted political company fifteen years ago.
Seventeen years ago.

speechtext:
I do not wish to drag
Colonel Domville's name into this discussion; Colonel Domville was the candidate of the Liberal party. As the campaign proceeded my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) began to see that his chances of election were not the best in the world, and so he wrote a letter to Mr. Sinnett who was president of the Conservative party in the county of Kings, in which he used language something like this:	in handing you back unsullied the banner of the Conservative party which the party in this county did me the honour to place in my hands, I desire to say I do it not because I have any difference of opinion with the Conservative party, whose policy I regard as essential to the well-being and progress of Canada, but in order that a candidate may be elected who will have a better chance of carrying the constituency than I will. The hon. gentleman's resignation, so gracefully tendered, was accepted, and another candidate was selected. Then shortly before the election, in the city ot St. John, there were two tickets representing the Conservative and the Liberal parties in the field, and suddenly my hon. friend emerged as the candidate of an independent party, the two planks in the platform of which were undying hostility to the action of the Conservative party in regard to the Remedial Bill, and the alleged grievance that the Conservative party had not done what it should to develop the port of St.'John; a fact which of course was known to my hon. friend at the time he was the candidate of the Conservative party in the county of Kings. We used to have joint meetings on nomination day, and I remember the joint meetings on that occasion very well. T remember standing in the court house and listening to the eloquent words of my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) as he told how he could not support the Conservative party because they brought in the Remedial Bill and because, forsooth, the Conservative party was^ not giving justice to the port of St. John. Then, he lifted his other hand and he said he had no confidence in Mr. Laurier, the leader of the Liberal party. Well, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) was nolj .elected;; he did not poll a very large vote, but ten days after the election, what do you think, the same hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) was about the most ardent Liberal you could find in any part of Canada.' The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugs-

ley) having referred to the circumstances under which we parted politically, I thought it well for me just to give to the House this little description of the reasons.

Would that be before
my right hon. friend the Prime Minister became a Conservative; I am not quite sure as to that?

speechtext:
I think you have your
hands full with your own case now.
It is time for him to change again.

Seventeen years is a
long time to go back, and I congratulate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries upon the care he has bestowed upon remembering my language. The fact that he has remembered it so accurately shows that he has repeated it a great many times during the past seventeen years. I certainly think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has never made in New Brunswick a political speech during all that time in which he has not repeated verbatim his remarks of this evening. No wonder the hon. gentleman is able to get it off so glibly and eloquently, so smoothly and
And correctly.

Yes, I think correctly.
I think there is no doubt that at the time he refers to I did decline the nomination in the county of King's.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But you accepted it, eh?

I withdrew from it and I did it in a very proper manner and in a manner which was quite acceptable to the people of the constituency. Not that they were glad to get rid of me, because I appealed to the people of Kings county a great many times and I always received a handsome majority from them; two or three times I was elected by acclamation and on other occasions I received majorities running from four hundred to eight hundred. My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) cannot say that I was unpopular in my native county. But, the hon. gentleman has forgotten one thing, and that is that the election in 1896 did not come off within a year of when it was expected, and when I accepted the nomination it was a year before the election and before the remedial order was pub lished.
Oh.

My hon. friend knows
that to be true. Do you think there was anything extraordinary in a man who entertained such strong views against the people of an independent province like Manitoba being coerced, should differ from the Conservative party, on so important a question which was then dividing the people of the different provinces. It was after the
remedial order was published that I became an independent candidate for the city of St. John, and it was before it was published that I was the Conservative candidate in Kings. Under what circumstances did I become an independent candidate? My hon. friend knows very well that the people of St. John, having faith in their port, urged its consideration upon the Government and public meetings were held and party ties thrown to the winds because the people felt they had been denied justice by the Government of the day.
Was the remedial order, to which the hon. gentleman refers, published at the time he wrote his letter withdrawing from the field as a Conservative candidate?

I am not able to tell
the hon, gentleman as to that. I can tell him that the remedial order was not published at the time I was in nomination. And, Sir, that feeling, as I have said, the feeling that the Government was not doing justice to the port of St.John had been growing, and at last it culminated in 1896, as my hon. friend knows. He knows that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) came to the city of St. John and was waited upon by representative citizens on both sides of politics. Certain demands were made upon him by the people of St. John that were right. He turned a deaf ear to the entreaties of the people, and my hon. friend knows the intense indignation which was aroused among the citizens of St. John. An independent party was formed. And my hon. friend knows that very strong Conservatives like Mr. W. Frank Hathaway, who was president of the independent party, and others, scores and hundreds of strong Conservatives, became members of that independent party. They asked me if I would run as the candidate of that party. Well, Sir, I owed nothing to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I owed nothing to the Conservative party; I was not a member of this House; I was a free and independent citizen; and 1 had a perfect right to take that course which I believed to he in the interest of my city and of my country; and I ran as an independent candidate.
What has all that to do with the Navy Bill?

My hon. friend from
Halton (Mr. Henderson) has wakened up and wants to know what this has to do with the Navy Bill. I am sure that many hon. members have wondered what it has to do with the navy and why the Minister of Marine and Fisheries entered at this time into this matter of seventeen years ago. It is true, I was not elected, but the

indignation of the people of St. John rested on my hon. friend the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and he and his colleague were defeated, showing that the . people at all events did not regard them as worthy of their confidence. At that time, seventeen years ago, the people of St. John taught the hon. gentleman a lesson, which, I trust, he has not forgotten. I think it was a salutary lesson. Perhaps to-day he has more ginger in him than in 1896, and is prepared to fight better in the interests of the people of St. John than he was at that time. I do not think he will ever forget the lesson the people of St. John taught him. 1 think it was a pity, that on this great question of whether we should build a Canadian navy or whether we should send $35,000,000 out of our country, away from our own people, depriving our own labouring men of the opportunity for profitable employment in building warships in order to make a contribution to the British Government, which does not need our money-I say, it is a pity that on this question of whether we should begin now a series of contributions which if once begun we cannot stop, an hon. gentleman occupying the distinguished position of Minister of Marine and Fisheries should turn aside to ask this House to consider whether or not, seventeen years ago, I acted properly and conscientiously in ceasing to follow and support my hon. friend upon the occasion to which he has referred. Would it be contrary to Parliamentary rules for me to say that such a course is unworthy of one occupying the position of my hon. friend? Do you, Mr. Chairman, honestly think that an hon. gentleman occupying such a position is justified in bringing in this irrelevant and unimportant matter before the House when the House ought to be engaged in considering what was at one time at least thought to be an important question-though that is a long time ago and interest in it has pretty well died out-do you think that on such an occasion one in the position of my hon. friend should interject the discussion of these matters of seventeen years ago? To me that time, seventeen years ago, seems a long time away. The only particular recollection I have of it is that the hon. gentleman was angry and chagrined then, as he seems to be angry and chagrined at the memory of the terrible defeat he then met.
I do not want to prolong this discussion, but as the hon. gentleman has spoken of a ' terrible defeat,' I may-say that I was beaten by 100 while my hon. friend lost his deposit.

But my hon. friend
ought not to forget to tell the committee that he was supported by the Conservative Mr. PUGSTjEY
party with all its influence and all its wealth, while I was simply the spokesman of a small independent body of electors with no great party behind us but simply fighting for a great principle, a small body~of citizens who did not regret defeat in the cause we had espoused. And, though my colleague and I were not elected to Parliament, the principles for which we fought were sustained by the people.

I am sure the committee has listened with great interest to the discussion which has occupied its attention for the last two hours. On one thing, I am sure, all will agree, and that is that the representatives of the constituency of St. John claim a good deal of the attention of the committee and of the House for the discussion of the political exploits and events in that constituency for the last twenty-five years. I am sorry that the Minister of Naval Affairs, whose duty in this naval discussion seems to be to talk about everything except naval affairs leaves the Chamber when an attempt is made to bring the attention of the committee back to the subject. I congratulate the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that he has been able to get his colleague, the responsible Minister of Naval Affairs to get up in this House and discuss this question, or at least attempt to discuss it. From the occasion on which, in answer to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, on December 12, last, the hon. Minister of Naval Affairs stood in his place and addressed to the House in a speech which had been either written by himself or prepared by somebody else, he has not ventured to give this House or the country any information such as a minister occupying that responsible position ought to give. When we on this side, sought from this Government that which we have a right to receive from them, the most full, complete and accurate information in regard to the subject, who was it that gave to the House what little information has been vouchsafed to us? Was it the responsibe minister? Sir, he never ventured, or ever was permitted to do so; the Prime Minister seemed to be the one and .only one on the Government side of the House and in the Government who had any knowledge in regard to this question. Why was it that the right hon. Prime Minister did not give to his colleague, the minister having to do with this matter, the responsibility of carrying this measure before the House? The Minister of Naval Affairs is a public man of many years experience; he sat in this House twenty years ago, and since that time has held a seat in the legislature of his own province and has been premier of that province. But the Prime Minister has

taken out of the hon. gentleman's hands from the beginning, everything in relation to the naval discussion, so that the hon. gentleman has not been permitted, up to this stage of the debate, to give to Parliament the information that every minister gives in relation to his department. Hence it is that when his colleague ventures upon a discussion of this question, he harks back to ancient history and tells once more this old story which we have heard so many times with regard to the political events in the city and county of St. John and the province of New Brunswick. What a pitiful position this is for the Minister of- Naval Affairs of this Government. After a lapse of more than six weeks, when we are asked to consider this matter seriously, we find the minister evading the issue and departing so far afield as he has done in the discussion to which we have listened during the last two hours. My hon. friend was boasting of the accuracy of his information in regard to the cost of certain vessels, and seemed to gloat over the fact that he had observed an item in a New York newspaper to the effect that the Fore River Shipbuilding Company of Quincy, Mass., had been sold <to the Bethlehem Steel Company. Does he not know that there are to-day eight or nine other large and prosperous shipbuilding concerns in the United States, engaged not merely in the building of battleships, but in mercantile and marine construction, and in the building of vessels for all parts of the world? I happen to have some special knowledge of the facts in regard to the Fore River Shipbuilding Company. Two weeks ago I visited my own country, and while there I met the relatives of a young man, a native of my county in the province of Nova Scotia, who to-day, after ten years absence from his native province, occupies the position of assistant engineer for the Fore River Shipbuilding works in Quincy, Mass. I w as told by his proud relatives that he is now in Naples, superintending the delivery of a vessel which was constructed for Italy in these works of which we have heard so much this evening. Instead of attacking the ability of Canada to engage in this industry, and alleging that there has been some failure in the United States in that connection, he should have taken the trouble as Minister of Naval Affairs to ascertain not only how many sons of Canada are engaged in the naval service of the United States; but how many natives of Canada, like this boy, Mr. Page, of the county of Pictou, have walked to the front ranks in naval construction, and are among the most successful men in the ship-building works of the United States. In order that we might have some more accurate information than we have been able to obtain from the hon. gentlemen opposite, I took the liberty of applying to a journalistic friend of mine in New York, who is a Canadian, with a view to ascertaining some real facts in regard to the cost of naval construction in the United States. I have received from him some figures which can be verified by reference to the United States Naval Annual, showing the cost of the vessels built for the navy of the United States within the last ten years. The plans for the armour, which were only then under consideration at that time by the United States Government, were of such a character that they1 contemplated the widest possible expenditure.
