The result is that my hon. friend the Minister of Naval Affairs, speaking for the first time since December the 12th upon this question, has given us information which is only $3,000,000 out as in regard to the cost of the particular vessel to which he refers. What was the object of my hon. friend the Minister of Naval Affairs in telling us that the Fore River Shipbuilding Company went into liquidation-an announcement which was cheered with enthusiasm by hon. gentlemen sitting behind him ? What is his idea in exaggerating the cost of the Pennsylvania, unless it be for the purpose of leading the House and the country to believe that the cost of construction of vessels on this side of the water is so great that business enterprises fail when they engage in that work, and that we should not undertake it ? If he can have any other motive for making that suggestion I would like to know what it is. The fact that there are to-day eight or ten huge, prosperous industries in the United States engaged in the manufacture of all kinds of vessels, about which there is no question whatever, is suppressed by the hon. member, nor has he given the figures which I gave, showing that the six last battleships built for the United States Government in their own country were built at a cost of less than $10,000,000. These are facts which are not given to the country by my hon. friend when he ventures to give us information. Why is this? Is it to show that we in Canada cannot do anything in the way of shipbuilding?
Possibly.

Are we to understand that the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in this debate is that suggestion that comes from the Opposition that this money might as far as possible be spent in Canada is one which should not be entertained for a moment because the Canadian people cannot engage in ship-Mr. MACDONALD.
building? Is that the policy? If that is the policy of hon.' gentlemen opposite it is a humiliating policy. I wonder what the former great leader of the Conservative party would say, the statesman who promulgated the national policy, who urged that out of our own resources here in Canada and by our own labour we should establish manufacturing conditions and that there should be a tariff under which the Canadian people would pay more for the articles which they purchased in Canada and would be penalized if they went abroad to purchase, all in order that we might inaugurate manufacturing industries in Canada. These hon. gentlemen do not believe in that policy evidently because if they did they would not be found making the arguments they make here. Every hon. gentleman who goes before the Canadian people and says: You must not, perish the idea, engage in the construction of steel vessels within the borders of Canada. Any man who says that is recreant to every principle which the Conservative party has ever advanced in this country since 1878, because if Canadian workmen and Canadian pluck and Canadian labour and brains cannot do what the same qualities possessed by other people and other nations of the world can do, surely Canada occupies a humiliating position. Yet that is where hon. gentlemen opposite, that is where the Minister of Naval Affairs is placed by all the little arguments he has ventured to make to-night. What does the Premier mean when he tells us, as he did on April 7, that this was not a free gift which he proposes. When this proposition was made on December 5 the headlines of every Conservative newspaper in Canada were marked by the -bold statement that Canada was bringing to the feet of the Motherland this free gift for the purpose of standing by her in time of need. That was the policy which the Prime Minister announced, that was the policy of the Conservative party on December 5, 1912. That policy was changed somewhat. The Premier made a curious speech on April 7 when you come to analyze it. He was trying to justify himself and to make the argument that he was consistent with his attitude on the resolution of 1909. He knew that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House charged him with inconsistency, that we claimed- that he, in common with every hon. gentleman in Parliament in 1909 had voted for a policy which we then declared was to be the permanent policy of this country, the lines on which we were to lay down our relations on naval affairs and aid the Mother Country and he naturally felt the force of the criticism made and attempted to justify himself. He read the resolution of 1909 and said:

I pointed out to the right hon. gentleman then, and my argument apparently prevailed with him, that conditions or urgency might so develop at any time that the very best course, and the safest course for Canada to pursue would be to make a contribution-although we are not even going that far to-day, because we are only proposing to expend $35,000,000 in the construction of ships which, although placed at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of the Empire, nevertheless will be the property and in the ownership of the Canadian people.
That was a new step in the journey upon this question, not a free gift, not a generous handing out of this money from the pockets of the Canadian people in order that the old Motherland should see that the heart of her Canadian subjects was as true and loyal to all the institutions that existed here. I would like my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to study that speech of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister goes on further:
He already knows from my statement and from the correspondence that has been brought down, that if it should hereafter be the will of the Canadian people to establish upon a permanent basis a great naval organization, the ships can be recalled upon reasonable notice whenever the people of Canada shall desire and so determine.
The Premier is not going to give this money to England, that is certain. Secondly, he is not going to give any ships to England, they are always to belong to Canada and they are always going to be owned by Canada. Both of these things are very widely different from the original proposition. But my hon. friend has a third proposition in regard to it. Not only is he not going to give the money or the ships but he is going to own the ships; he will lend them to be used in this flying squadron, not in the North sea at all, they are going to be loaned until Canada makes up her mind that she will have a navy of her own. That presupposes logically that it is possible to build ships in Canada and for Canada to have a naval organization of her own. That is a fair deduction from that proposition. If Canada is only going to loan ships to England in the meantime until she establishes a navy of her own, I say that presupposes that Canada can do what we say to-day she can and ought to do, that is have ships built and owned and controlled here in Canada. So that the Prime Minister is contemplating a condition of affairs and assuming that it will be brought about in the very near future, the very conditions that we say ought to be hastened at this moment. Does he propose to bring them back to Canada before they become obsolete? I assume that if he has any idea on this question, and I know that his thought in the back of his head, if he was free to do so, would be to get up to-night and declare that the proper attitude for Canada is to go on the line of Canadian-owned vessels, a Canadian-owned navy, and to build the vessels as far as possible in Canada. That is his permanent policy. Those ships that the Prime Minister is going to have built in England must be brought back before they get obsolete. There is no doubt about that, otherwise he is misleading this House and the people of Canada. All right. This subject is a very interesting one, Mr. Chairman, and on that account I would not like to vote on clause* 2 without having something to say on the subject. It is particularly interesting because of the wide differences of opinion that seem to exist on the other side of the House as to the policy of the Government so far as present requirements are concerned, and also as to the policy of the Government in the future. Those differences of opinion seem to grow as time goes on. Some weeks ago, or perhaps I should say some months ago, there was a strong feeling on the part of a great many Conservatives that there was needless obstruction in this House. There were many Conservatives who charged that the Opposition were obstructing the conduct of business. However, there was a large number of Conservatives who shared the opinion of Liberals that the obstruction was producing a great deal of good, inasmuch as it was throwing some little light on the darkness which seemed to overshadow hon. gentlemen on the right of the Speaker, during the greater part of the winter. If you read the speeches on the other side, and if, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kings, you take the speeches of the Prime Minister himself, delivered on 5th December and on 12th April and attempt to reconcile them you will have a difficult proposition in hand. If you take his views and contrast them with the views of some of his followers in regard to the policy which the Government has in mind, you will find just as much difficulty in reconciling them. However, there seems to be one view that controls the party opposite, and that is the view of the Montreal Star. If one can judge from what their press says, the Montreal Star and the Toronto News have this Government pretty well in band. They pull the strings and the Government has to dance to their music. The Montreal Star has come out most unequivocally in support of the view that the only policy for Canada is a policy of permanent contribution. That is the effect of the arguments which the Montreal Star has been putting up during the winter. It is true that hon. gentlemen opposite try to make it appear that this policy of sending $35,000,000 out of the country is not a permanent policy. That is a very large sum of money, and the people of Canada, irrespective of politics, look upon it as a sum of money which could be more profitably utilized in this country. The people of Canada regard the sending of this money out of the country as a very serious matter, and one and all they condemn the sending of it out of the country unless it can be shown that there is a serious reason why it should be sent. Had a proposition of this kind been made when the German scare was on some years ago, or even last September, or October, -when the Montreal Star had the country worked up to fever heat over the imaginary emergency that existed in Europe, perhaps the people of Canada might have been disposed, if not to view with favour the contribution of $35,000,000, at all events to condone the sending of the money out of the country. But thanks to the Opposition and to the so-called obstruction, which was not obstruction at all, the people have had time to reflect, and they now see that there is no such thing as an emergency. They have discovered that the conditions in Europe are seemingly of the most pacific character, and that there is nothing whatever to justify the suspicion of any estrangement or of any ill-feeling between England and Germany. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) the hallucination of an emergency has disappeared, and to-day there is none so poor as to do reverence to an argument of that kind. The Montreal Star is most emphatic in saying there is only one policy for Canada, a policy of permanent contribution, and it ridicules the idea of having a Canadian navy at present or in the future, for, after all, that is the effect of .the articles of the Star. If you read and weigh them carefully and dis-

passionately, you will find that the whole argument of the Montreal Star is that we must embark on a policy of permanent contributions, and we find an echo of that in the statement of the Prime Minister himself. What does he mean when he criticises hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and when he asks:	What are
you going to do with your fleet units on the Atlantic and Pacific; of what earthly service are they going to be in time of war; what do you want them for anyway? And he says that such fleet units are unnecessary when we have such a splendid organization in Great Britain to protect our shores and commerce. On some occasions he makes strong appeals and strong arguments to show that as there is only one flag and one King there should be only one navy. He takes the ground that a Canadian navy is absolutely useless, and that for Canada to embark upon a policy of that kind would be very unwise. That is his argument.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says
' hear, hear.' Do I understand him to say that he does not believe in a Canadian navy?
Most decidedly not.

It is refreshing to
find an hon. gentleman who at this late hour says he does not believe in a Canadian navy, but there were other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House-I do not know the names of their constituencies, but there are some within hearing of me-who said that their policy was not a policy of permanent contributions, that the. present contribution was to meet an emergency, a pressing need, and that a Canadian naval policy would be embarked upon later, when the scheme could be properly developed and matured. However, my hon. friend from Peterborough does not take that view of it. He is one of the disciples of the Montreal Star. Evidently he has been imbued with the idea that in Canada we are not able to build a navy of our own, and that the only way in which we can discharge our duty to the Empire is by permanent contributions.
That is not my idea.

That policy has been enunciated by the leader of the Government himself, and let me call the attention of my hon. friend from Peterborough to the fact that when the Prime Minister took that ground he qualified his statement by saying that we could not embark upon a policy of contribution unless we had a voice in the councils of the Empire, unless we had a say in the making of war and peace. He said that no self-respecting Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
country like Canada would for a moment think of contributing year after year or from time to time to the exchequer of England unless it were given representation in the councils of the. Empire, and he sought to convey the impression that when he was in England last year he secured representation of some kind. But that bubble was pricked a very short time after the House met. The letter of Mr. Harcourt, the Colonial Secretary, would seem to have been a reply to the speech that was made by the right hon. leader of the Government in which he alleged that he had secured representation for Canada in the councils of the Empire. That letter disproved the argument completely and showed that any representation that Canada was to have was not any new representation that had been offered to the present Government, but that it was something that had been offered to the late Administration some years ago and which did not give us any say in peace or war. It would simply be that the representative of Canada would be there in an advisory capacity and nothing more. In further substantiation of that I might quote the words of the First Lord of the Admiralty himself, and of other British statesmen, to the effect that an arrangement such as that which has been suggested would be absolutely impossible. I had the honour myself of quoting from a statement by Sir Joseph Ward in which he pointed out the difficulties of an arrangement of that kind, and in which he declared that it would be impossible to carry out any such arrangement. At the Colonial Conference of 1909, the representatives of the various colonies discussed the question of representation in Imperial councils, and the present Prime Minister of England, who presided at that conference, stated that a scheme of that kind was absolutely impossible. The matter has been discussed again and again in this House, and no hon. gentleman on the other side has attempted seriously to argue that the scheme was feasible. Everybody knows that the voice we would have in the Imperial Council would be so feeble that it would be almost insulting to the pride and ambitions of Canada to be represented there.
Then so far as the question of an emergency is concerned, that argument has been knocked into a cocked hat. Nobody takes the emergency seriously. There is nobody who will pretend that there is a situation in Great Britain to-day which calls for a contribution of .$35,000,000. If there was an emergency, if there was any real danger to the Empire, the people of Canada would not hesitate to vote, not $35,000,000, but four or five times that amount, if necessary.
Do I understand that the hon. gentleman, in view of the fact that he considers there is no emergency, would refuse to send over anything ?

No, I never said any
such thing. I say that we have duties to perform as a part of the Empire, and the resolution of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition points out how! these duties should be performed. He says that he would undertake the defence of this particular part of the Empire, and that in providing for the defence of this part of the Empire, along the lines laid down some years ago by so illustrious a Conservative as Sir Charles Tupper, and along the lines laid down by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce- (Mn Foster) and the right hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Borden) when they were in opposition, we are doing our duty towards the Empire. We could do something effective for the Empire by pursuing that course. But the course that we are asked to pursue is not going to be in accord with the wishes of Great Britain, and it is not consistent with the self-respect of a colony such as Canada is. There is no emergency and there is no .reason for giving this $35,000,000 to the lords of the Admiralty.
On what ground then can you put this grant at $35,000,000 ? It is not that Great Britain needs it. This morning I read in the Ottawa Citizen, a good Conservative authority, the following:
Given under compulsion, Canada would not receive its money's worth, there being no real compensating gain to the country or to the Empire. Great Britain does not need Canadian money. She is amply able, by reason of her wealth to supply all the battleships required for naval defence. Unless Canada's money means Canada's heart and sentiment, the proposed action can mean little more than the transference of several tons of gold from the public treasury into the armament barons' private purse.
Let me quote to you some statistics regarding the wealth of Great Britain, I am quoting from the Kingdom Papers, vol. 15. Whilst hon. gentlemen on the other side may not agree with everything that the writer of these Kingdom Papers says, they will all concede that he is one of the cleverest men in Canada. He .says this:
Q. Is the United Kingdom in need of cash?
A. -No. She has command of unlimited revenues. Part of the income of every civilized man in the world (and of many of the uncivilized) goes, directly or indirectly, every year to pay interest upon her investments. Her new foreign investments last year were over $800,000,0(>0. Her present foreign investments are about $18,000,000,000. Her annual increase in wealth is about $1,200,000,000. Besides paying for all her military and naval preparations, her old age pensions, and everything else, she has repaid, in the last five years, on account of her national debt (due almost entirely to foolish wars) over $270,000,060. Her national debt is about two-tliirds that of France; and her national wealth is one-third greater.
It is unnecessary to dwell upon the financial standing of England, or to make
any comments on what our paltry $35,000,000 would mean to England in a case of this kind.
Our hon. friends opposite, and particularly my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), lay a great deal of emphasis on the cost of building ships in Canada? I observed that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries took very good care not to give a straight, definite and categorical answer to the question put to him by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) when he was asked if he thought that these smaller vessels, cruisers and warships, could not be built in Canada. He wisely evaded that question and he evaded it by answering that it is not possible to build dreadnoughts in Canada. Nobody contends for a moment that dreadnoughts can be built in their entirety in Canada at present. As the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) has said, everything must have a beginning, and,in the matter of building warships, we must make a beginning some day or other. It is idle to pretend we cannot build ships in Canada. Is there anything in our climatic conditions; are our people so inferior, so lacking in intelligence and capacity, that we cannot build ships. We have the iron, the steel, the nickel, the men, the brains, the muscle, the money; we have everything required and there is no reason why we cannot engage in this industry as well as any civilized country in the world. True, it may cost a little more to build these ships, in Canada than in England where they have established shipyards doing business for a great many years, but does that argument come with good grace from gentlemen on the other side. Are our artisans and labourers entitled to no consideration from them? They have to pay heavy duties on everything they use and why not avail of this opportunity to assist our industrial and farming community by creating a ship-building industry, thus giving them a chance to earn the money to pay the extra cost on what they consume? The artisan can buy his clothes and other necessaries of life cheaper in England than in Canada, but this 'beneficent Government will not let him do that without taxing him heavily for the privilege. Even if it should cost more to build ships in Canada-and it will cost probably more for the first few years-does it lie in the mouth of hon. gentlemen opposite to

[DOT]say that because of that fact the ships taiust be built on the other side, especially when these gentlemen maintain a high tariff against the consumers of the country. I might quote from the remarks of the Prime Minister who, speaking at Halifax on October 14, 1909, told the people that the ships should be built in Canada; that in 1909 all parties were in accord on the policy of having a Canadian navy, and he called upon the people to appreciate the fact that he was a true Canadian in advocating this policy. I can quote also from Mr. George Drummond of Montreal, a very eminent authority, to the effect that the ships should be built in Canada. Bet it is not necessary to go further than to point out the fact that when tenders were invited for the construction of strips in Canada, six ol the most responsible and largest shipbuilding firms in the world tendered to build the ships here, and they put up a large money deposit to show their good faith. The very fact that the advertisement calling for tenders stated that the ships should be built m Canada, and should be approved by the Admiralty, and that six large firms tendered to do the work in Canada sets at rest once and for all the contention that it was not possible to get the ships built here. In 1909, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster) pointed out in eloquent terms the great advantage that would result from building the ships in Canada, and that argument is as sound to-day as it was then. If the hon. member (Mr. Foster) was here tonight, I am sure he would not be found contending that we could not build ships in Canada just as well as they can in any other part of the world. I have here a little book on Canada which points out some of the things which our country possesses, and iit affords interesting reading. It shows that Canada possesses the largest consecutive wheat field in the world; the most extensive sea fisheries in the world; the largest nickel mine in the world; a greater railway mileage than Australia, New Zealand, Italy and Spain combined, and more than all the South American countries; the greatest railroad system in the world, the Canadian Pacific Railway employing 73,000 men; the largest grain mill in the British Empire; the largest elevator in the world at Port Arthur; the longest bridge span in the world at Quebec; one of the largest single canal locks in the world at Sault Ste. Marie; the largest lift-lock in the world at Peterborough; the largest coal field in the world at Stellar-ton, Nova Scotia. Surely a country that possesses such great things is able to start in the ship-building industry, modest perhaps at first, hut ultimately able to build Mr. CHISHOLM (AntigonishV
the largest warships afloat. Other countries have navies and why should not Canada? For my part I am not enthusiastic over military or naval expenditure, and I think a great many of the people of Canada entertain the same view, hut as a country attains the status of nationhood, it has to assume the responsibilities of police protection, avid such things as an army and navy are necessary evils. Other countries are building navies; the United States shipyards are turning out war vessels; China, Japan, Norway, Sweden, are able to assume responsibility in this regard, and surely Canada ought not lag behind. The question at issue between the two parties is not whether Canada is ready and willing to undertake her obligations of contributing to the defence of the Empire, but simply as to the method. The policy of the Government, so far as I have been able to gather from what I have heard in this House and read in the press of hon. gentlemen opposite, is a policy absolutely uncertain; they do not know themselves what their permanent policy is. The Montreal Star is fixed in one view-it must he a policy of contributions . But some hon. members opposite, apparently a majority, do not subscribe to that doctrine but indignantly repudiate the idea that such is *their permanent policy. They sav theirs is a policy of a Canadian navy. Why, then, do not they tell us wherein the policy of the late Government Act and the present naval law are defective and just what their policy is. This is the time. There is no emergency now; there is no hurry. Why does not the leader of the Government take the country into his confidence? If .there were danger of war there might be reason for an emergency policy, the permanent policy to be announced later. But it is four yeaTs since the German war scare was started, and as years roll by the danger of war between England and other great countries of the world becomes less and less. According to leading statesmen of the Empire, conditions improve week by week. Is it not time for the Government to be more frank in the matter and declare, if it be true, that their policy is one o.f permanent contribution? I move the adjournment -of the debate.
